item.title: Apple Backports Fix for Exploited CoreGraphics Flaw to Older iPhones and iPads (2026)
item.description:
Apple on Monday backported fixes for a high-severity security flaw that was exploited in real-world cyber attacks to older devices.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-86950 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write affecting CoreGraphics that could result in arbitrary code execution when processing a maliciously crafted file.

Patches for the flaw were released last month by Apple in versions iOS 26.7.1, iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1, acknowledging that it may have been exploited in sophisticated attacks against specific individuals using devices running iOS before iOS 27.

The fixes have now been expanded to include iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11, which support iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later.

"Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27," the company said.

iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 also address a logic issue in Audio (CVE-2026-65339) that could be exploited by an app to leak sensitive user information and an access vulnerability in CoreMedia (CVE-2026-86990) that could be abused by a malicious app to access the camera without user permission.

The release comes as Apple shipped iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS Golden Gate 27.2, tvOS 27.2, watchOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, and Safari 27.2, fixing hundreds of vulnerabilities, including many in AppleAVD, CoreAudio, ImageIO, kernel, Model I/O, Screen Sharing Server, Spotlight, StorageKit, and WebKit.

Notable among the defects is an authorization issue in Apple Intelligence (CVE-2026-86987) that could be exploited by a remote attacker to access sensitive user data. The iPhone maker said the issue was addressed in iOS and iPadOS with improved entitlement checks.

Although Apple makes no mention of any of these flaws being exploited in the wild, it's always a good practice to update the devices to the latest version for optimal protection.

item.title: GoAhead TLS Flaws Allow Revoked Client Certificates and Enable Session Decryption (2026)
item.description:
The GoAhead embedded web server loaded a certificate revocation list into its default TLS backend but never turned revocation checking on, so a revoked client certificate could still pass login on affected setups.

The flaw is in builds that use the OpenSSL backend with mutual-TLS, where the server checks a client certificate and vice versa, and a revocation list is configured to block revoked certificates.

That is a setup an operator turns on deliberately; a default build does not. GoAhead 6.1.1, released to device makers on August 2, 2026, and publicly published on October 12, fixes it.

GoAhead is a small web server that device makers build into firmware to run management pages on routers, printers, gateways and industrial controllers. Its maker, EmbedThis, says it runs in hundreds of millions of devices.

The flaw was found by Sébastien Féry of FoxIO, who described it and two other TLS problems in a write-up on October 26.

On an affected build, the server loads the revocation list file at startup and reports no error, so an operator who configured it has every reason to think revocation is working. It is not. A client whose certificate was revoked, for example a stolen or retired device, completes the handshake as if the certificate were still valid and gets whatever access that identity allows.

In FoxIO's test against GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2, a revoked certificate was accepted with issuer checking switched on.

The OpenSSL advisory describes revoked client certificates as silently accepted. To be exploited, the build must use the OpenSSL backend with client certificates required, a trusted certificate authority bundle and issuer checking enabled, and a revocation list configured; the attacker must hold a certificate signed by a trusted authority and listed as revoked. Builds that use the Mbed TLS backend are unaffected; that backend checks revocation via a separate code path.

The identifier on the advisory is CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1 by EmbedThis. As of October 27, that identifier and the others below were not yet live in the public CVE and NVD databases; EmbedThis says it has requested them. The severity ratings are the vendor's own.

Researchers cover two further problems, each tied to a specific TLS build. The versions and fixes differ, so the table below maps each by backend.

TLS build What goes wrong Affected versions Fix or interim option
OpenSSL (default) Revocation list loaded but never enforced; revoked client certificates accepted. CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1. 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 Upgrade to 6.1.1. No interim option in the advisory.
LibreSSL legacy verifier (3.2.x, 3.3.2–3.3.6) A client certificate chain longer than the limit is accepted when client certificates are required but issuer checking is off. CVE-2026-115884, rated 7.4. 6.1.0 and earlier on those LibreSSL versions Upgrade to 6.1.1, or turn issuer checking on with a trusted CA bundle, or use OpenSSL or LibreSSL 4.x.
Mbed TLS A length typo sends a 1-byte Diffie-Hellman value instead of the full 2048-bit one, so a passive observer can decrypt the session. Rated 5.9. No CVE assigned. 4.0.2 through 6.1.0 Upgrade to 6.1.1, turn off finite-field DHE suites, or use the OpenSSL backend.

The Mbed TLS problem only reaches a session if the client accepts the broken setup. OpenSSL, current Go, current Java, and mainstream browsers refuse a value that small and fall back to a stronger key exchange, so the session never completes.

Clients without a minimum-size check, such as some embedded or custom ones, accept it, and then anyone who recorded the traffic can work out the key and read the session. TLS 1.3 and ECDHE sessions are unaffected, and Mbed TLS 4.x removed the key exchange they rely on.

The LibreSSL problem allows an attacker to present a certificate chain longer than GoAhead's 10-certificate limit and still complete the handshake as an authenticated client, without any trusted key.

It appears only on builds linked against the older LibreSSL versions listed above and only where client certificates are required with issuer checking off. OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC and LibreSSL 4.x reject the over-long chain.

Which backend and settings a build uses are chosen when the firmware is compiled, so a device owner cannot tell from the outside which apply. That is also why the fix is slow to arrive: GoAhead 6.1.1 is a drop-in replacement that device makers rebuild and ship as a firmware update, and an owner gets it only when their manufacturer does so. Whether any manufacturer has shipped it is not known.

As of October 27, no source reported any of these problems being used in attacks. EmbedThis's policy is to end a disclosure embargo and publish early if a flaw is being exploited or disclosed by someone else, so the coordinated October 12 release is consistent with no known attacks. 

However, it does not prove there are none. EmbedThis notifies customers of security updates through its Builder portal. FoxIO has published proof-of-concept code and offers fingerprints through its JA4Scan tool to find GoAhead servers by backend. The tool is free, but its source is available only on request, and a fingerprint identifies a build, not a confirmed-vulnerable server.

None of the device makers EmbedThis lists as GoAhead users, which include HP, Oracle, Siemens, Canon, Rockwell, D-Link and Comcast, has been shown to run an affected backend and setting. The affected population is not established.

The same 6.1.1 release closes 11 advisories in all, three of them rated critical. One is a login bypass: on a build using HTTP Basic or form login, an attacker who knows a valid username can sign in with any password if that user's stored password is in the newer Blowfish format, which GoAhead added in version 6.1.0. EmbedThis says form login is the default for its built-in administration pages.

After upgrading, EmbedThis recommends ending active sessions, restarting the server, and changing Blowfish-stored passwords.

item.title: CyberStrikeAI Uses 44 AI Agents to Automate Hacking Operations Against Japan Targets (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of three cyber attacks targeting organizations in Japan in which artificial intelligence (AI) was a key element, either in the driving seat or to assist a human operator.

TrendAI, which analyzed three exposed server environments used by threat actors to conduct the malicious cyber operations, described them as distinct from previously published attacks that have leveraged ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration testing framework, to single out entities in South Korea and Japan.

"These environments held reconnaissance and attack tools, scripts, target lists, results, logs, and command histories," security researchers Bakuei Matsukawa and Joseph C Chen said. "They ranged from workspaces used largely by hand by skilled operators to AI-agent platforms that automated the entire workflow, including command and control."

The first of the three attacks has been found to abuse CyberStrikeAI, another open-source penetration testing tool that was previously put to use in an attack campaign targeting Fortinet FortiGate appliances. The activity was concentrated in a short period in October 2026.

The AI-driven activity leverages the offensive security tool to automate various aspects of the attack lifecycle into a repeatable workflow,  beginning with reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery and validation, and exploitation, to command-and-control (C2), persistence, data exfiltration, and automated reporting.

This involves delegating the work among 44 agents to handle various aspects of the attack, while also enabling the generation of forms and fake login pages in the Japanese language.

"In a short period, at least 19 identifiable organizations, including at least 16 in Japan, were subjected to validation activity," Trend Micro's enterprise security division said. "Each had a report in the same format and an index of evidence. These were outputs of a structured process run by the platform, rather than ad hoc notes left by an operator."

The second case has been characterized as a human-led attack with assistance from a large language model (LLM) to accelerate planning and tool development. Analysis of the infrastructure and artifacts indicates that the campaign is also designed to target AI workflow platforms and inference services with an aim to obtain large amounts of inference capacity at low cost.

One of the intrusions is said to have targeted a geographic information system (GIS) server exposed with default credentials, resulting in the theft of cadastral and commercial records, Windows credentials, and email data. The entire campaign lasted for 24 days in August and September 2026.

The third instance is where the AI's role has been found to be confined to developing the operator's tools and scripts, suggesting a limited role played by the technology in a series of campaigns designed to target edge devices from Cisco, Citrix, F5, and Yamaha using published vulnerabilities, management functions, or credentials present in configuration files.

The threat actor is estimated to have run at least six campaigns from January to October 2026, opportunistically striking exposed VPN devices and WebLogic servers. "The operator was experienced, with established practices for automation and evidence management," the researchers said.

There is currently no evidence at this stage that suggests these three incidents share an operator. It's also unknown if the attacks have targeted other regions and what AI models are being used to pull off the attacks.

That said, the attacks involving these threat actors are not restricted to Japan and neighboring countries like South Korea. The operator behind the first case has targeted organizations in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while the third case featured organizations in the U.K., France, Italy, Qatar, and Colombia in its WebLogic discovery lists.

"AI has increased the attackers' workforce, but the work still consists of looking for unlocked doors," TrendAI said. "The types of doors and the weaknesses that leave them open have not changed. What has changed is the ability to try thousands at once, adapt to the target country's language, and continue without fatigue."

The development coincides with the discovery of multiple campaigns in which threat actors of varied motivations have integrated agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows, allowing them to speed up research, malware development, social engineering, and other parts of an attack.

To make matters worse, AI is being increasingly used to accelerate reconnaissance, automate decision-making, and industrialize social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation of security flaws. According to Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, AI has collapsed the median time from vulnerability discovery to weaponization to well below 24 hours.

The adoption of AI by bad actors is reducing the time, expertise, and cost required to discover and exploit weaknesses, at the same allowing attackers and defenders alike to operate with greater speed, scale, and autonomy, the Windows maker added.

"The key issue is not simply whether an actor has frontier AI," Trend Micro said. "Access to capable models can already produce meaningful operational gains. Ecosystem depth, however, determines how reliably, independently, and at what scale those capabilities can be sustained."

"AI is no longer an experimental capability for APT groups; it is an operational component embedded directly into campaigns."

The growing demand for AI tools by threat actors has also opened up a new monetization avenue that peddles stolen AI provider session tokens and offensive AI tools APEX AI, MessiahGPT, and DarkGPT, further commoditizing cybercrime and lowering the barrier to entry for carrying out advanced, persistent, and evasive attacks.

Last week, Microsoft revealed that a China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used ARTEX to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. The activity has been attributed to Storm-0940, which it said has used the framework since as early as September 2026 to automate password-spraying attacks on hundreds of organizations.

"While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," Microsoft said. "Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations."

According to local media reports from South Korea, authorities have identified seven suspects linked to a cybercrime operation that broke into more than 90 organizations in the country, most of which involved ARTEX. The 32-year-old mastermind behind the activity is alleged to have worked at a cybersecurity company between 2019 and 2022, gaining expertise in penetration testing.

In 38 of the incidents, the threat actors demanded ransom payments of 360 million won ($270,000) in exchange for not leaking the stolen data. More than 8.2 million records are believed to have been siphoned from compromised organizations.

Some of the other AI-oriented campaigns that have been documented in recent weeks are listed below -

  • A financially-motivated threat actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor as a secondary tool (both with safety controls disabled) to run a WordPress brute-force campaign against an Indian university's website and generate a REST API enumeration report.
    • The attacker also breached a second Indian public university, exfiltrating a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students. A third attack enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform to extract a storefront API token, admin email addresses, phone numbers, and payment merchant IDs.
    • "The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders)," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations."
  • An e-crime group named CyberCartel has been observed using a multi-agent system called CARLIY0S to coordinate attacks against banks and payment providers across Latin America. The framework employs a cognitive swarm comprising four role-specialized Claude models that "debate each target and defer to one arbiter" before the main orchestrator acts. "The group assigned different roles to commercial AI models to analyze targets, develop attacks, and coordinate operations," Straiker said.
  • Threat actors have developed an offensive AI agent designed to hijack exposed AI endpoints to run autonomous attacks, with instructions allowing it to carry out up to 100,000 steps without human approval while the legitimate owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. The system features a malicious loop called Skynet mode that employs a set of 74 tools to scan for targets, infect them, deploy cryptocurrency miners, and reinfect compromised hosts.
  • An affiliate for the The Gentlemen ransomware operation has used Anthropic Claude Code during intrusions into at least six organizations in late June 2026, including to generate and execute reconnaissance and exploitation commands, write malicious scripts, modify firewall policies, and identify high-value business systems.
  • A credential-harvesting operation codenamed Zerofot built a scanner named "auto_scan" that integrated OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to harvest thousands of API keys and tokens from thousands of exposed hosts across the internet.
  • An AI-generated Python framework called RAGE has been used to scan internet-facing services (e.g., Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, Apache Tomcat, Jenkins, Hadoop YARN, Confluence, and Supervisord), exploit vulnerable deployments, capture credentials, and deploy cryptocurrency miners.
  • A human operator employed frontier AI models to breach an enterprise network autonomously over a 10-hour period. "The actor breached a publicly accessible web service to tunnel into the network, deploying an automated recon agent to map internal microservices," Unit 42 said. "Sub-agents combed enterprise code repositories, extracting hard-coded tokens and service passwords." The attacker then harvested master administrative credentials and hijacked an enterprise code application to exfiltrate cloud access keys. The stolen cloud keys were then used to turn the victim's AI endpoints into post-compromise infrastructure.
  • A suspected Russian-speaking cyber actor used an AI-assisted workflow to exploit PaperCut NG/MF servers and compromise hundreds of instances. "The campaign extended beyond initial exploitation into a structured post-exploitation pipeline covering Windows credential collection, service-credential harvesting, internal network pivoting, Metasploit automation, and victim packaging," Hunt.io said.
  • A Chinese-speaking threat actor has breached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, using an autonomous penetration testing engine called Cairn, tasking it to probe targets, search for security weaknesses that could lead to code execution or account takeover, attempt to break in, and steal sensitive data.

"AI is serving as a force multiplier and an expanding attack surface at the same time," Rapid7 said. "Generative AI is accelerating established attack methods by reducing the time, skill, and coordination previously required to execute them at scale."

"Rather than introducing entirely new categories of exploitation, threat actors are integrating AI into existing workflows to industrialize phishing, automate reconnaissance, and refine malicious scripts with greater speed and precision."

item.title: Adobe Commerce PolyShell Attacks Breach Hundreds of Stores as Brotli Exploit Traffic Emerges (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added two vulnerabilities impacting Adobe Commerce and Magento, and Google's Brotli decoder library to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.
  • CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) - An unrestricted upload of a file with dangerous type vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session.

The development comes days after Sansec said it observed attackers leveraging CVE-2026-48356, also known as PolyShell, to breach hundreds of e-commerce stores to inject a malicious loader via a Magento CMS block.

The loader is designed to fetch and execute an attacker-controlled payload, although no next-stage malware has been recovered to date, making it challenging to determine what the exact goals of the campaign are. The activity is assessed to be ongoing since at least July 2025.

As for CVE-2026-111497 (aka Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell), telemetry data from threat intelligence firm Previdian shows that one exploitation attempt has been recorded against its honeypot sensors from a U.S.-based IP address as of October 27, 2026. It's currently not known if these efforts are broad in scope.

"An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory," Rapid7 said. "According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder."

ELLIO also reported on Monday that its sensors "have recorded CVE-2026-111497 exploit traffic in the wild, carrying the public exploit that we confirmed gets a shell on vulnerable builds." The activity originates from "94.154.43[.]7," an IP address geolocated to the Netherlands that has also engaged in exploitation efforts targeting PHP2Shell, two critical flaws in PHP that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution.

"The attacker's payload is a genuine, correctly-structured Node2Shell exploitation attempt for node v24.22.0 – the Brotli stream, staged displacement, pivot pair, and delivery are all correct and identical to the public tooling," ELLIO said. "This is indicative of the RCE being adopted by an operator focused on mass exploitation."

The fact that Brotli is a widely distributed open-source library and adopted by numerous projects has provoked an emergency response, prompting various vendors to release patches or assess if their products are affected by the flaw.

This includes PHP, which has shipped versions 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, and 8.2.35-1, as well as Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, Python, ClickHouse, the PHP Brotli extension, and the Ruby "brotli" gem. Links to some of the advisories are below -

  • Amazon Linux
  • Broadcom
  • Bun
  • Cisco
  • Cloudflare
  • CloudLinux
  • Envoy Proxy
  • F5
  • Fortinet
  • Imperva
  • Istio
  • Microsoft Azure
  • Microsoft .NET
  • Node.js
  • Palo Alto Networks
  • PHP
  • Qualys
  • Red Hat
  • Safe Security
  • Strapi
  • Tanium
  • Tenable
  • Ubuntu
  • Upwind

"Node.js fixed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1," Akamai said. "The Node.js advisory does not offer a workaround, so upgrading is the only complete remediation. Organizations running a discontinued release line should move to a supported release line."

Google-owned Wiz has warned that "91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances."

"Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli," Sysdig said. "Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability."

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 10, 2026, to apply the necessary fixes against the two flaws.

item.title: ShinyHunters-Exploited Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day Turns Out to Be Three Chained Flaws (2026)
item.description:
The critical Oracle PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May is not one flaw but three chained together, the researchers who reported it said this week.

Oracle patched all three under a single identifier, CVE-2026-35273, in June. Its root is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches an internal management interface because PeopleSoft trusts its own loopback address by default, opening the door to remote code execution without a login.

The breakdown comes from Bobby Gould of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), whose team reported the flaw to Oracle.

In its analysis, ZDI said it reported three distinct vulnerabilities across two PeopleSoft components, and that it is working with Oracle to assign a separate CVE to each. As of this week, the one June identifier is still the only one on the record.

CVE-2026-35273 affects PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62, carries a CVSS score of 9.8, and lets an unauthenticated attacker take over the server over the network. Oracle released its fix in an out-of-band security alert on June 10. The flaw is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

Attackers were already using it before that fix was in place. Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) attribute a campaign to the group it tracks as UNC6240, better known as ShinyHunters, that exploited the flaw between May 27 and June 9, mostly against universities. Because that activity came before Oracle's June 10 advisory, it was a zero-day the whole time.

In a September follow-up, Mandiant reported a renewed, larger wave that spread beyond education to technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transport, and government, affecting dozens of systems worldwide.

ZDI's analysis explains what that single patch actually closed. Two PeopleSoft components are involved, both run as separate web applications. The Integration Gateway (PSIGW) exchanges messages with outside systems. The Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) is an internal admin interface that is supposed to answer only to trusted hosts.

The first flaw is the SSRF in PSIGW. An attacker sends a request to its listening connector and controls both the address it forwards to and the full payload it sends, ZDI said; the handler does no check that the destination is a legitimate target. That alone would be limited, except for what it can reach.

PSEMHUB decides who to trust by checking the requester against a list in a file named allowedhosts.properties. That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list. So an attacker points the SSRF at 127.0.0.1, the request arrives looking like it came from the machine itself, and the trust check passes. The internal interface Oracle meant to wall off is now reachable from outside.

From there, ZDI described two ways to turn that access into code execution. One abuses a PSEMHUB command meant to write log entries: the caller controls both the file contents and the exact path on disk, so an attacker writes a web shell into the application directory and runs commands as the PeopleSoft service account.

The other writes a malicious XML file that PSEMHUB reads using Java's XMLDecoder when the service next starts, thereby running the attacker's code without planting a web shell at all. The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.

The design decision at the center, ZDI said, is that allowing loopback access by default makes the trust check ineffective once the SSRF exists. That matters for defenders who thought a firewall rule had covered them.

In the September wave, Mandiant found ShinyHunters slipping past web application firewall (WAF) rules that blocked the /PSEMHUB/ path by url-encoding a single character, requesting /%50SEMHUB/ instead. Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page.

What to Do

The fix and the guidance here come from Oracle and Mandiant, not from ZDI's analysis, which covers the flaw rather than the response.

  • Apply the patch. Install Oracle's security alert fix for CVE-2026-35273 and stay on a supported PeopleTools release. Mandiant is explicit that path-based WAF blocking is not a substitute for patching.
  • If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub service in multi-server setups, or remove the PSEMHUB application in single-server setups, as Oracle's alert advises. Restricting these admin endpoints does not break normal user sessions.
  • If you may already be hit, Mandiant recommends treating any host with a web shell as compromised, preserving evidence, and rotating every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier. ShinyHunters steals data and then demands payment, so affected organizations should prepare for extortion.

One thing the sources do not settle is whether applying the patch removes access an attacker already gained. Oracle's alert does not address it, and Mandiant's guidance to rotate credentials and hunt for web shells assumes it does not. Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

item.title: Tailscale Patches SSH Flaws That Could Let Hacked Devices Gain Root Access on Other Servers (2026)
item.description:
Tailscale has released version 1.104.4 to fix flaws in its built-in SSH server that could let an attacker reach services and files on other servers that only the root user should be able to touch.

The flaws are in how Tailscale SSH forwards network connections, a job the Tailscale background process carries out with root privileges. To use them, an attacker must already control a device that the network's access rules permit to open an SSH session to the target, with forwarding allowed in that rule.

The flaws come from a report called Tailworm, published days before the fix by Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs, who tested released versions of the Tailscale client and the self-hosted headscale control server in a lab.

Tailscale SSH decides who can connect using a device's identity and the network's policy file, not a password or key, so an attacker does not need stolen credentials, only a foothold on a device the policy already trusts.

The flaws "don't allow an unauthenticated attacker to connect to arbitrary Tailscale SSH servers," Tailscale said, and an attacker can still reach only the machines the policy file already allows.

Tailscale SSH's server runs only on Linux and the open-source macOS build; the attacker's own device can be any platform.

The problem is in socket forwarding. When a permitted SSH session forwarded a connection to a Unix socket on the server, the Tailscale process checked the path but then operated as root. A timing trick let an attacker swap in a different path after that check, defeating the safeguard meant to limit which sockets forwarding could reach.

In Windisch's own tests, forwarding to the Docker control socket produced a root shell and read the system password file, /etc/shadow, with no administrator rights. Tailscale's bulletin describes the reach more narrowly, saying an attacker could get to root-only sockets such as the Docker socket or the tailscaled local API.

In 1.104.4, Tailscale changed the server to carry out forwarding as the logged-in user rather than as root, and to rely on the operating system's own file permissions in place of its earlier path check. The release covers 4 security bulletins:

  • TS-2026-014: the SSH socket-forwarding flaws above, which let a permitted session reach root-only sockets such as the Docker socket or the tailscaled local API.
  • TS-2026-015: a way for a permitted SSH session to use up a server's memory and crash the Tailscale process, cutting all Tailscale networking on that node.
  • TS-2026-016: a flaw in tailscale serve where a forward to a Unix socket could reach the tailscaled local API, giving remote control of the node, plus a related socket-swap issue.
  • TS-2026-017: a flaw where, with TLS serve and 2 or more mounts, one request could receive another mount's permission headers.

What to Do

Users of Tailscale SSH should update to version 1.104.4 or later. If you cannot update a server yet, you can turn off SSH forwarding on it by setting TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restarting the service, which Tailscale says turns off forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH and blocks several of the more serious findings.

Tailscale also recommends reviewing SSH access rules so that only the users and devices that need access have it.

Tailscale suggests using SSH check mode, which requires a user to sign in again before a session starts, for sensitive systems. Check mode does not stop these forwarding flaws: it guards the start of a session, whereas the forwarding occurs within a session that has already been approved.

If a server may already have been compromised, Windisch's report says the fix alone is not enough. A stolen device key stays valid until the device is deleted at the control plane, because reimaging the machine does not revoke it. Tailscale's notices do not cover this case.

The picture is worse on headscale, the self-hosted control server. On headscale, SSH forwarding is granted on every accepted session and cannot be turned off in the policy, so Windisch's report says every SSH grant there should be treated as giving root. The newest headscale release, version 0.29.5 from October 13, does not fix the reported issues.

Is It a Worm?

Windisch called the chain "wormable." In her tests, one compromised device could spread to every device the policy allowed, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step.

Two controls stopped the spread in those tests. Writing access rules as single device-to-device pairs held it back, and binding device keys to hardware such as a TPM kept a stolen identity from being reused elsewhere.

Tailscale rejected the worm description. The findings do not describe self-replicating malware that spreads between machines on its own, the company said, but lateral movement limited to the connections a policy file already allows.

It called the privilege-escalation problems "serious security issues," said it had reproduced the main ones, and added that it is still working out which configurations are affected.

Disclosure and Earlier Fixes

As of publication, the 4 bulletins carry no CVE identifiers or severity scores, and none state the oldest affected version. The report also covered Tailscale's app connectors and its serve and funnel features.

Tailscale said the app-connector finding is in conn25, an experimental feature it has not released, and that the connectors customers use today are not affected. Of 5 serve and funnel findings, it fixed 3 and said the other 2 work as designed.

Windisch published the report without coordinating the release with Tailscale first, which she has described as "reported but not coordinated." Tailscale said it received the report on the morning of Saturday, October 24, about 2 hours before Windisch published it, and that its engineers were already looking at the same parts of the code.

Neither Tailscale nor the report says the flaws have been used in real attacks. The proof-of-concept code is not public, and Windisch said she gave it only to Tailscale's security team.

The report is the latest in a run of fixes in the same part of Tailscale this year. In June, Tailscale fixed a separate flaw in Tailscale SSH's Unix-socket forwarding that let an unprivileged user reach a privileged socket, in version 1.98.9.

Windisch called the chain "wormable." In her tests, one compromised device could spread to every device the policy allowed, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step.

Two controls stopped the spread in those tests. Writing access rules as single device-to-device pairs held it back, and binding device keys to hardware such as a TPM kept a stolen identity from being reused elsewhere.

Tailscale rejected the worm description. The findings do not describe self-replicating malware that spreads between machines on its own, the company said, but lateral movement limited to the connections a policy file already allows.

It called the privilege-escalation problems "serious security issues," said it had reproduced the main ones, and added that it is still working out which configurations are affected.

Disclosure and Earlier Fixes

As of publication, the 4 bulletins carry no CVE identifiers or severity scores, and none state the oldest affected version. The report also covered Tailscale's app connectors and its serve and funnel features.

Tailscale said the app-connector finding is in conn25, an experimental feature it has not released, and that the connectors customers use today are not affected. Of 5 serve and funnel findings, it fixed 3 and said the other 2 work as designed.

Windisch published the report without coordinating the release with Tailscale first, which she has described as "reported but not coordinated." Tailscale said it received the report on the morning of Saturday, October 24, about 2 hours before Windisch published it, and that its engineers were already looking at the same parts of the code.

Neither Tailscale nor the report says the flaws have been used in real attacks. The proof-of-concept code is not public, and Windisch said she gave it only to Tailscale's security team.

The report is the latest in a run of fixes in the same part of Tailscale this year. In June, Tailscale fixed a separate flaw in Tailscale SSH's Unix-socket forwarding that let an unprivileged user reach a privileged socket, in version 1.98.9.

item.title: Japan's GMO Offers $1 Million Bounty to Catch Hackers Behind FX Trading Cloud Breach (2026)
item.description:
Japan's GMO Internet Group is offering up to $1 million in total for tips that help catch the attackers who breached its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service, after refusing to pay an extortion demand.

The reward program opened on October 28 and pays only if a tip helps lead to an arrest or an international wanted notice. The service hosts Windows desktops used for FX trading, and a broker has linked unauthorized trades on some of its customers' accounts to logins leaked from the service.

GMO says the attackers took customer information. It received a demand for about $50 million (about ¥8 billion) on October 21 from people it believes carried out the attack. They have also threatened its customers' trading accounts and data.

On October 27, the attackers posted material on their website that they say is information about GMO and its customers. The site's domain, including its mirror sites, was shut down at about 4 a.m. Japan time on October 28, and GMO plans to act against any new site.

How the Reward Works

GMO Internet Group runs and pays for the program, called GMO Cybercrime Bounty. Tips are sent by email to an address listed on a dedicated website, in Japanese, English, or Chinese, and can be anonymous. The program is open until an arrest, an international wanted notice, or October 27, 2027, whichever comes first.

GMO wants information linking people, servers, domains, IP addresses, accounts, or cryptocurrency addresses to the attack, extortion, or movement of money, along with evidence of how the crimes were carried out. Guesses, unsupported accusations and reposts of public information generally do not qualify.

A tip earns money only if it leads to an arrest, including one by police outside Japan, or to an international wanted notice, such as an Interpol Red Notice. GMO decides how much each tip helped, and one tipster can receive the full $1 million or the total can be split. Tipsters must prove their identity before payment, and if no tip qualifies, no payment is made.

Some people cannot be paid, including anyone involved in the crime, anyone who got information illegally, such as by buying leaked data, and GMO staff. GMO tells tipsters not to break into systems, negotiate with or pay the attackers, or send leaked data, credentials, or malware.

Tips are shared with police and other authorities in Japan and abroad as needed. GMO has already given police all its evidence on the threats, including communication records.

GMO will never ask tipsters for passwords, authentication codes or fees, and it writes to them only from addresses ending in @cybercrimebounty.gmo.

The Breach and the Trading Accounts

GMO Internet, the subsidiary that runs the service, found on October 20 that a third party had installed malicious programs on some customers' servers. It shut down the servers on every plan from October 21. It counts 26,739 servers as potentially affected, which is not the number of confirmed break-ins or data thefts.

On October 24, GMO said it had confirmed a security problem in the service's systems, unauthorized access to the service, and the exfiltration of customer information from the company.

Anything customers stored on the servers may have been viewed, including login credentials saved in trading software such as MetaTrader 4 and 5 (MT4/MT5). GMO does not keep customers' payment card data on the servers.

Customers began reporting trades they did not recognize on October 21. A broker, OANDA Japan, has confirmed that a third party logged in to and traded on some of its customers' accounts using ID and password pairs it believes were leaked from the GMO servers. It has restricted trading on accounts that may be affected, and as of October 26 it had not found a break-in or leak in its own core systems.

Another broker, FXTF, warned on October 22 that third parties may have stolen the logins of some customers who use VPS servers, in an attack it believes hit another company's VPS servers. They may also have used the logins to log in and trade. It told customers who had connected to Desktop Cloud to change their FXTF passwords from a device that had never connected to it.

GMO Internet Group said in a stock exchange filing on October 28 that it had not yet confirmed how many customers its payments will cover, how much information was published, or which trades qualify for compensation. It had not confirmed any impact from the breach on its other services.

The Threats and the Leak

GMO says the attackers threatened to keep manipulating customers' accounts at more than 70 securities and FX firms, to publish information about the service and about customers' PCs, to hit those PCs with ransomware, and to publish details of GMO's systems.

They set noon on October 27 for publishing customer information and launching the ransomware attack. No ransomware attack had been confirmed as of 1:55 p.m. Japan time that day.

The material posted on October 27 was what the attackers called one customer's personal information, ITmedia NEWS reported that afternoon. GMO was checking it that day.

The attackers collected information about anyone who visited their site, according to GMO, which tells visitors to run a full antivirus scan. It asks people not to visit the site or any new one, and not to repost or link to the material.

How the Attackers Got In

As of October 28, GMO had not said how the attackers got in.

Masatoshi Kumagai, who heads GMO Internet Group, wrote in an October 25 blog post that the group's own white-hat hackers had warned the team running the service about problems in advance.

The response was neither fast nor thorough enough, he wrote, and the attackers took advantage of the gap.

On their website, the attackers claimed that one administrator account was shared across all the servers and that customers' PC drives were visible from the servers by default when they connected, ITmedia NEWS reported.

They also claimed they used a flaw in the service to reach customers' own PCs. GMO had not publicly confirmed these claims either.

By October 26, GMO had collected PCs from customers who offered them for analysis, as of 11:59 a.m. Japan time on October 27, it had found no malware, including ransomware, on the PCs it had finished checking. That does not confirm that every customer's device is safe, and the analysis is still ongoing.

What Customers Should Do

GMO has told Desktop Cloud customers to take these steps:

  • Change trading-account and trading-software passwords from a device not used for FX trading, such as a phone.
  • End every logged-in session, through the broker if needed, even after changing the password.
  • Check trading history and balances, and report unrecognized trades to the broker first.
  • Turn on two-factor authentication where the broker offers it.
  • Change passwords reused on other services or saved in the browser.
  • Run a full antivirus scan on devices used to connect, and back up data.
  • Do not reply to messages from anyone claiming to be behind the attack, or open their links or files.
  • Ignore offers to recover lost money for a fee. GMO will never ask for a password or authentication code.

GMO Internet will pay every current user ¥5,000 and cover actual trading losses and fees from trades it confirms were unauthorized and caused by the breach. Customers whose information it confirms was published will also get ¥10,000 to ¥25,000 for each type of information exposed.

GMO will not restart the service on the breached systems as they are. Customers who want a Windows desktop will be offered a move to a separate service, free for six months and only with their consent, with details due by October 30.

item.title: FBI Seizes Virtualine Domain Over Alleged Criminal Hosting and Bitcoin Money Laundering (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine.

The move was in response to the service being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct," the DoJ said.

Visitors to the "virtualine[.]net" domain are now greeted by a message that states it has been seized by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation as part of a coordinated operation between international law enforcement agencies and private sector entities, including the Hessen State Police, the National Police Corps of the Netherlands, the U.K. National Crime Agency, OverRIPE, and Lumen Technologies.

According to court documents, Virtualine, which also operated as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums, claiming that they can be used for phishing, carding, email spam, and port scanning, with the exception of child content and terrorism activities.

In June 2025 on HackForums, the provider is alleged to have boasted that "Virtualine ignored more abuse than your last three therapists." Earlier this March, it also began marketing an "additional protection plan" that promised its customers to move their criminal infrastructure to a shell company unaffiliated with Virtualine when receiving official requests from law enforcement agencies.

Snapshots captured by the Internet Archive show that standard plans cost anywhere between $19.99 per month for one virtual CPU, 2GB memory, and 30 GB storage to $179.99 per month for 24 vCPUs, 64 GB memory, and 130 GB memory. Virtualine also offered plans optimized by CPU, memory, and storage, starting from $21.99 per month to $379.99 per month.

"Despite advertising that it does not allow 'child contents' on its server, Virtualine knowingly hosted a website that did so, identified in court records as Vendor 1," DoJ said. "Vendor 1 is a criminal online forum that allows users to post and sell access to nude, sexually suggestive, and/or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults."

"Vendor 1 also promotes a hack-for-hire service in which users can pay hackers to access victims’ online accounts without their consent and illicitly obtain explicit images and videos. In January 2026, about one month after Virtualine assigned an IP address to Vendor 1, Virtualine began receiving notifications about sexually explicit images and videos of minors on that server."

The Justice Department said Virtualine continued to host Vendor 1's services despite receiving numerous notices from law enforcement in Germany, Canada, and Australia; the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in the United States; and a victim's attorney.

Virtualine has also been accused of working closely with Vendor 1 to create a new website where its clients could upload their illicit content and download it upon completing a purchase. The website continues to be hosted by Virtualine to this day, the department added.

"Virtualine.net included a number of payment options for Virtualine's customers, including Vendor 1," the DoJ said. "Virtualine accepted payment through BTC [NO-AML], specific unhosted bitcoin addresses that allowed customers to direct pay without concern their funds would be flagged as illicit."

"The funds Virtualine's criminal customers paid to Virtualine, some of which can be traced directly to various criminal groups, were received by Virtualine and then further laundered to conceal the origin of the funds."

Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, in its own analysis, said Virtualine accepted direct Bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without triggering compliance checks at hosted exchanges.

"Virtualine's on-chain footprint has direct exposure to a broad cross-section of the cybercrime ecosystem, including ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses," it said.

Following the site seizure, the operator of Virtualine has published an open letter, refuting allegations that the service knowingly hosted child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The operator also claimed they have taken action on requests for cooperation concerning CSAM within 24 hours. In a post shared on their Telegram channel, they insisted that customer data was safe.

"When we identified prohibited material associated with the customer described as 'Vendor 1,' we ended our relationship with that customer," the individual added, claiming "Virtualine has been part of my life for five years."

"Please do not cast suspicion on me and the tens of thousands of customers who have trusted Virtualine because of the actions attributed to a single customer. I want you to know that I am prepared to respond to your requests concerning 'Vendor 1.'"

In September 2025, the Spamhaus Project revealed that Virtualine had expanded their operations to AS209800. "Thanks to Turkey- and U.S.-based IP address brokers with poor customer vetting procedures, Virtualine keeps obtaining new IPv4 prefixes for enabling internet abuse. AS209800 is currently routed via aurologic GmbH, a hosting provider proliferating several other bulletproof hosting operations."

"A lost ASN does not by itself mean the BPH has stopped," Silent Push said. "The speed of acquiring a new ASN is a crucial part of the problem, and we believe the process for registering an ASN should be tougher."

Update

According to an analysis published by TRM Labs, Virtualine received more illicit-attributed cryptocurrency than any other labeled bulletproof host in 2026, surpassing SecureHost, vpsbg, F0XYF0X BPH (aka Bearhost), and Gerry, despite lower total inflows.

A Russian drug marketplace accounted for nearly 44% of direct inflows, while a large sextortion scheme, a mixer, and ransomware groups were responsible for about 17%, 13%, and 5%, respectively. Direct payers include Coinbase Cartel, The Gentlemen, INC, DragonForce, and Qilin, alongside malware operators such as the StealC infostealer and the Matanbuchus loader.

Other counterparties that have transacted with Virtualine are darknet markets, illicit goods and services operators, bot and malware-distribution services, and sites linked to child sexual abuse material.

"Virtualine is another example of Russia's illicit economy at work: darknet markets, ransomware groups, non-compliant exchanges, and brokers all feeding the same ecosystem," Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, said in a statement shared with The Hacker News.

"Bulletproof hosting is the connective tissue. Seizing a domain matters, but the blockchain record doesn't disappear with it. It shows who is paying, who is getting paid, and where they go next."

A press release from the Dutch police has revealed that dozens of physical servers located in a data center in Limburg were seized in Limburg, taking hundreds of virtual servers offline.

"Through the seizure, the police are in possession of data and information relating to more than 3,000 customers who used the servers for criminal activities," the Politie said. "The secured data will be used for further police investigation regarding customers who used these servers for criminal purposes."

As of October 29, 2026, virtualine[.]org, the domain that hosted the open letter, and the Telegram channel are no longer accessible.

item.title: Anthropic's Unreleased AI Model Chains Flaws Into Working Chrome, Safari, Windows and Linux Exploits (2026)
item.description:
An unreleased Anthropic AI model found security flaws in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux and chained them into working proof-of-concept exploits, the company said in its latest report.

The exploits were built in the lab after the model was prompted, not seen in any real attack, and Anthropic reported every flaw to the vendor first, so all of them are already patched. One proof of concept opened the Calculator app on a stock Mac running Chrome within seconds of a page loading, with no further clicks.

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described five chains in a research post. The strongest claim is not any single bug, but that one model found several separate flaws and combined them into a working exploit, something the company says has until now been the work of a few specialist teams. That capability claim rests on Anthropic's own account.

The patches and the fact that Apple and Google credit Anthropic and its Claude model for specific fixes can be verified with the vendors.

What a reader cannot check is how much of each chain the model built on its own. Anthropic says the work needed only "initial prompting" and "little human involvement," but it does not break down what a person did at each step, and it does not name the model beyond calling it an unreleased, internal research model.

For the one flaw with its own public record, the Windows bug, the record names no finder at all. Here are the five chains, what each would do, the condition each needs, and where the fix landed.

Platform What the exploit does Condition it needs Fix
Chrome Runs code on the computer, outside the browser's sandbox, from one visit to a web page One click or page load, stock Chrome on macOS Chrome 156, October 20
Safari Lets any website read data from other sites the user is signed in to, such as email or a bank account One visit to a malicious page iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2, June 29
Android Copies photos and other data off a locked, stolen phone Physical access to the phone, over USB Anthropic says Google has fixed it; no public record was found
Windows Crashes a server over the network, and keeps it down by repeating The server answers HTTP/3 requests CVE-2026-33096, patched April 2026
Linux Runs commands as root over the network, with no login and no user action The server runs a multipath TCP listener CVE-2026-98432, patched October 15

In the Chrome chain, the model used four separate flaws in turn. A malicious page first corrupted memory in V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine.

A second flaw escaped V8's memory sandbox and took control of the part of Chrome that renders the page. A race condition in a feature called CacheStorage then let that code read memory it should not reach and learn the layout of the more privileged browser process.

A final use-after-free bug in FedCM, Chrome's sign-in feature, let the exploit run code outside the sandbox entirely. Anthropic says it reported 62 flaws to Google that were assigned CVEs and fixed as of Chrome 156, all rated critical or high, including 13 sandbox escapes.

Google's own release notes credit "Xinyang Ge of Anthropic, assisted by Claude" for specific Chrome fixes, though not for all 62.

item.title: American Organizations Under Attack: Skyw4lker Device Code Phishing Campaign Exposed (2026)
item.description:
Modern phishing campaigns can compromise American businesses without relying on traditional credential theft. Attackers can abuse legitimate cloud services, authentication mechanisms, and trusted business workflows to gain access to corporate accounts while leaving fewer obvious signs behind.

ANY.RUN's analysis of Skyw4lker, a device code phishing campaign primarily targeting U.S. organizations, shows how this works in practice. The campaign has focused on manufacturing, technology, and healthcare, using business-themed documents, Google-hosted infrastructure, and Microsoft authentication flows to facilitate account compromise.

For security teams, the investigation goes beyond identifying the initial lure. It requires tracing the authentication flow and supporting infrastructure, extracting reliable indicators, and turning those findings into detections that can protect the wider organization.

Device Code Phishing: A Growing Challenge for U.S. Organizations

The scale of phishing in the United States provides an important backdrop. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded 193,407 phishing and spoofing complaints in 2024, making it one of the most frequently reported categories of internet crime. In 2025, the FBI recorded more than 1 million internet crime complaints and $20.9 billion in reported losses, with reported losses increasing by 26% compared with the previous year.

Attackers are also adapting to organizations that have invested heavily in identity security and MFA.

Device code phishing is one example. Rather than collecting credentials through a fake login page, an attacker can initiate a legitimate device authorization flow and convince the victim to complete it. The resulting authentication tokens can then provide access to resources available to the compromised account.

How Skyw4lker Uses Legitimate Authentication to Compromise Accounts

How the Skyw4lker Campaign Works

Skyw4lker starts with a lure designed to resemble normal business correspondence, as observed in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox analysis.

The Skyw4lker phishing kit identified in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox

Victims receive a password-protected document presented as a contract or service proposal. The scenario is credible in environments where employees routinely exchange vendor agreements, procurement documents, statements of work, and similar files.

From the document, the victim is directed toward a page hosted on sites[.]google[.]com, which eventually leads into a Microsoft authentication flow.

Skyw4lker redirecting the victims to a Microsoft365 authentication page

The attacker does not need to reproduce Microsoft's login experience perfectly. The authentication itself can be legitimate; the deception is in convincing the victim to complete an authentication request initiated by the attacker.

Once the process is completed, the attacker can obtain access to the resulting Microsoft 365 tokens.

That makes the attack difficult to evaluate through identity telemetry alone. An organization may see a valid authentication event without immediately seeing the malicious context that caused it. Establishing what happened requires the security team to connect the document, web activity, authentication flow, and associated infrastructure.

The Infrastructure Behind the Skyw4lker Phishing Page

The web infrastructure used by Skyw4lker provides additional evidence of the campaign's operation.

ANY.RUN’s analysis identified obfuscated JavaScript and a PHP backend used to create a victim session, collect information such as IP address and geolocation, and repeatedly poll the backend while waiting for the authentication process to complete.

Skyw4lker sample submissions in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox by country

A static inspection of the original document may reveal the starting URL, but it cannot fully explain what happens once the victim interacts with the page. The malicious behavior emerges through the combination of browser activity, JavaScript execution, backend communication, redirects, and authentication.

That makes behavioral analysis essential when the objective is to establish exactly what a phishing campaign is doing and which indicators can be trusted for follow-up detection.

View the Skyw4lker analysis in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox to see its complete attack chain and associated IOCs.

Reduce Tier 1 workload by up to 20% and give analysts more time to focus on critical threats.

Boost Your SOC Efficiency

Interactive Sandboxing Turns Suspicious Files and URLs into Actionable Evidence

An interactive sandbox lets security teams safely execute and interact with suspicious files, links, and documents, revealing behavior that static inspection can miss.

That matters in campaigns such as Skyw4lker, where the document is only the starting point. Analysts need to follow the attack through the browser, observe redirects and authentication activity, inspect network communication, and identify the infrastructure behind the phishing flow. All of this can be done in an isolated ANY.RUN Sandbox environment, with a result available in as little as 40 seconds.

The Tier 1 report for the observed Skyw4lker sample available in ANY.RUN’s sandbox

Instead of stopping at a malicious/benign verdict, the investigation can produce URLs, domains, IP addresses, network activity, screenshots, behavioral evidence, and other IOCs. These findings give security teams the context needed to validate an alert, scope-related activity, and create detections from evidence gathered during a single investigation.

As a result, SOC and MSSP teams can reach a confident verdict faster without manually reproducing the attack across multiple tools, while the resulting intelligence can support threat hunting and detection across the wider environment. Moreover, the same workflow makes it easier for MSSPs to investigate new campaigns and turn findings from one customer case into intelligence that can be searched across other environments.

Turning Threat Intel into Earlier Detection

The value of an IOC increases when it can be used to detect another attack.

ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds) provide malicious IPs, domains, URLs, and contextual information derived from sandbox investigations. 99% of unique, high-confidence IOCs are added to TI Feeds after validation, helping security teams work with intelligence that has already been reviewed.

ANY.RUN TI Feeds provide live threat intelligence for real-time attack detection

ANY.RUN’s internal analysis found that up to 30% of unique malicious IOCs discovered in Interactive Sandbox sessions had already been observed by the company and were present in TI Feeds. When one of these indicators appears in customer telemetry, it can potentially be matched against existing intelligence before an analyst manually investigates the associated sample.

This creates a more efficient workflow: known malicious activity can be identified earlier, while sandbox analysis provides the behavioral evidence needed to investigate unfamiliar threats.

For internal SOCs, this can reduce time spent researching indicators that are already known to be malicious. For MSSPs, the same intelligence can help identify related activity across multiple customer environments. This is how the existing threat knowledge can be reused instead of reconstructed for every new alert.

Cut MTTR by 21 minutes and give your SOC more time to focus on critical threats.

Integrate TI Feeds

Threat Intelligence Provides Context Behind the Alert

An indicator becomes more useful when security teams can understand the activity surrounding it.

ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup (TI Lookup) allows analysts to investigate a suspicious domain, IP address, or URL and examine its history and associated activity. In a Skyw4lker-related investigation, this context can help determine whether an indicator is connected to the campaign, has appeared in other malicious activity, or requires further investigation.

In addition, ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Reports (TI Reports) provide a broader perspective by connecting indicators with campaigns, infrastructure, techniques, and observed behavior. This can reveal relationships that are difficult to see from individual alerts, such as multiple incidents sharing the same infrastructure or a suspicious domain belonging to a wider phishing operation.

When it comes to organizations in U.S. healthcare, manufacturing, and technology, those connections can be especially important. A compromised Microsoft 365 account can expose sensitive communications, intellectual property, operational information, and regulated data, making early identification of related activity critical.

How to Make Each SOC and MSSP Investigation More Valuable

A successful investigation should improve an organization's ability to detect the next attack.

For an MSSP investigating a suspicious contract sent to one American manufacturing customer, indicators associated with Skyw4lker can be searched across other customer environments and incorporated into monitoring. The same approach works within an internal SOC environment, where an IOC found after one employee reports a phishing document can be compared against historical telemetry to identify other potentially affected users.

ANY.RUN supports these workflows through API/SDK, STIX/TAXII, SIEM, TIP, and XDR integrations, allowing intelligence from investigations to feed into existing detection and monitoring processes.

The result is broader protection from the same investigation: an incident affecting one user can generate intelligence that helps identify related activity across a SOC or MSSP's wider customer base.

Uncover up to 58% more threats and gain broader visibility into emerging attacks.

Boost Threat Detection

Conclusion

Skyw4lker shows why modern phishing defense requires visibility beyond the initial lure or login page. By combining interactive sandboxing, threat intelligence, and contextual investigation, security teams can move faster from suspicious artifact to actionable intelligence and broader detection.

For organizations in the U.S., that means faster investigations, less repetitive manual work, and a better ability to identify related activity before it becomes a larger incident. The goal is not only to understand one attack, but to turn every investigation into protection against the next one.

item.title: Adobe Fixes 8 Critical Campaign Classic Flaws Allowing Code Execution and Security Bypass (2026)
item.description:
Adobe has released patches to address multiple critical security flaws in Campaign Classic that, if successfully exploited, could result in arbitrary code execution, security feature bypass, and privilege escalation.

The list of eight vulnerabilities is as follows -

  • CVE-2026-104351 (CVSS score: 9.9) - A code injection vulnerability that could lead to arbitrary code execution.
  • CVE-2026-104353 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An operating system code injection vulnerability that could lead to arbitrary code execution.
  • CVE-2026-105780 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An incorrect authorization vulnerability that could lead to arbitrary code execution.
  • CVE-2026-105489 (CVSS score: 9.9) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.
  • CVE-2026-105781 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.
  • CVE-2026-104350 (CVSS score: 9.3) - A reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability that could lead to privilege escalation.
  • CVE-2026-104354 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.
  • CVE-2026-105779 (CVSS score: 9.1) - An SQL injection vulnerability that could lead to security feature bypass.

The issues affect Adobe Campaign Classic versions 7.4.4 build 9402 and earlier for Windows and Linux. They have been patched in version 7.4.4 build 9403.

Also resolved by Adobe is a critical code injection flaw in Adobe Connect Desktop and Mobile for Windows, macOS, and Android (CVE-2026-48360, CVSS score: 9.6) that could result in arbitrary code execution.

The vulnerability has been fixed in the following versions -

  • Adobe Connect Desktop - 
    • Windows: version 2026.9.61
    • macOS Silicon: version 2026.10.66
    • macOS Intel: version 2026.10.170
  • Adobe Connect Mobile for Android version 4.5

Adobe said it's not "aware of any exploits in the wild for any of the issues" addressed in the update. Users are advised to update to the latest version for optimal protection.

item.title: Wazuh and AI for Enhanced SOC Workflows (2026)
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of this decade's defining technologies. From healthcare and finance to manufacturing and education, organizations increasingly rely on AI to automate repetitive tasks, uncover patterns hidden within large datasets, and support faster decision-making. Cybersecurity has experienced a similar transformation. While attackers employ AI to automate cyberattacks and accelerate vulnerability discovery, defenders are adopting AI to improve threat detection and enhance incident response.

Security Operations Centers (SOCs) receive a high volume of alerts from endpoints, cloud workloads, network devices, identity providers, and business applications. Although SIEM and XDR platforms provide visibility into these environments, analysts often spend considerable time correlating alerts, searching documentation, and determining the next investigative steps. AI offers a practical way to augment analysts by providing contextual explanations, summarizing findings, and recommending remediation actions, rather than replacing human expertise.

Challenges facing modern SOCs

Modern SOCs are expected to detect and respond to sophisticated threats while processing millions of security events every day. High alert volumes contribute to analyst fatigue and increase the likelihood that critical events are overlooked. Investigations frequently require switching between dashboards, documentation, vulnerability databases, and threat intelligence feeds before a complete picture emerges. As infrastructures become increasingly distributed across on-premises and cloud environments, maintaining consistent situational awareness becomes more difficult. AI-assisted workflows help address these challenges by reducing repetitive analysis, adding context, and accelerating investigative decision-making.

Wazuh and artificial intelligence for enhanced SOC workflows

Wazuh promotes flexible AI adoption through the Wazuh AI Analyst available on the Wazuh Cloud and integrations with third-party AI providers. Organizations can leverage the Wazuh AI Analyst capability on the Wazuh Cloud for guidance on their environment's security posture. Organizations that self-deploy Wazuh can also leverage Wazuh integrations with AI providers. The following sections highlight further details:

The Wazuh AI Analyst

The Wazuh AI Analyst is automated and hands-off. It is an AI-powered security analysis service for Wazuh Cloud subscriptions that processes your security data through Amazon Bedrock and Anthropic’s Claude, delivering insights without any manual configuration. It periodically emails key indicators, a histogram of protected endpoints, alert volume, active vulnerabilities, and a posture summary with a full PDF report attached. 

The reports are generated on your Wazuh Cloud subscription’s schedule and are periodically sent to your registered email address. You can also view them from the Wazuh Cloud console in the Environments > AI Reports page.

On privacy, subscription data is not shared with third parties and is not used to train AI models; it is processed only to generate your reports, with encrypted transmission, isolated processing, and no permanent storage. As with any AI output, the recommendations are advisory and should be validated against your own policies before you act.

Threat hunting and security operations with external AI integrations

Beyond the Wazuh AI Analyst, you can expand Wazuh capabilities using a self-hosted LLM and externally managed AI integrations tailored to your needs.
