item.title: Critical 16-Year-Old UEFI Flaw Can Run Code Before Secure Boot on Network-Booting Servers (2026)
item.description:
A critical 16-year-old flaw in EDK II, the open-source code that most hardware makers use to build UEFI firmware, can allow an attacker to run code on a machine before its operating system loads, but only while the machine is booting over the network.

UEFI firmware is the software that runs first when a computer is switched on, before the operating system. An attacker who can reach the machine with a crafted network message during such a network boot can hang the boot, or, with work tailored to the exact firmware build, run their own code before Secure Boot and other startup defenses load.

An attacker needs no password and no existing access to the machine, but does need to reach it over the network during the short window when it is booting this way.

Red Hat and SUSE, which both ship the affected code, rated the flaw as one an attacker exploits from an adjacent network position rather than across the open internet.

TianoCore, the project behind EDK II, published an advisory on October 22 and rated the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, 9.5 out of 10. A code fix exists, but no stable release of EDK II contains it yet, and the advisory still lists no patched version, so most users have nothing to install today.

What the Flaw Lets an Attacker Do

The flaw is a buffer overflow in EDK II's network-boot code, known as PXE. During a PXE boot, a machine loads its startup image from the network instead of from a local disk.

As part of this, the PXE driver listens for ICMP error messages and the small status messages that network devices send back, and copies each one into a fixed 504-byte area of memory.

The size checks in that copy are wrong in both the IPv4 and IPv6 versions of the code, so a message longer than 504 bytes spills past the area and overwrites nearby memory with data the attacker chose.

To set this off, an attacker only has to send one crafted error message to the machine's address while it is in the middle of a network boot. No password or existing access to the machine is needed.

The simple result is a crash: the boot hangs, and the machine fails to start. Getting code to run is much harder and far less reliable. The advisory says that an attacker who knows the exact firmware build can plant a "counterfeit event" that causes the firmware to run the attacker's own code, so an exploit has to be built for a specific build.

When code runs, it executes within the firmware, before Secure Boot and other boot-time checks have verified anything. That timing is what makes the flaw serious.

Code planted this way runs only once and does not survive a reboot by itself. That single run is still enough to install other code that does start on every boot.

Who Is Affected

The bug sits in EDK II up to and including edk2-stable202608, the newest stable version, dated August 21. EDK II is the reference code that nearly every UEFI firmware vendor builds on, including the independent BIOS makers AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, as well as Microsoft's hardened fork, Project Mu.

The flawed copy loop has been in the code since a commit added in November 2010, The Hacker News found by tracing the project's history.

PXE network boot is turned on by default in EDK II's standard build. The flaw does not affect home or office users who boot only from a local disk. It applies to organizations whose machines boot over a network, primarily servers and data center equipment.

How many shipping products carry the vulnerable code is not known. Intel told Ars Technica that none of its "commercial products currently under security support" are known to be affected, and that it "does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code," though an OEM board vendor or system maker could add it.

Arm said the flaw "is not directly applicable to Arm's product portfolio." Both companies' own firmware draws on EDK II.

Linux distributions also ship the code. Red Hat lists its edk2 package in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10 as affected and not yet fixed, and SUSE and Debian mark their equivalent packages the same way.

AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon did not answer the tech news site's questions before publication, and TianoCore did not respond either, so the status of their products remains unclear.

Is There a Fix?

A fix has been merged into the EDK II source code. It rewrites the faulty copy so an oversized message is cut off at 504 bytes instead of spilling over, and it reached the main development branch on October 15.

No stable release of EDK II includes that fix yet. The Hacker News checked the project's release tags on October 28 and found the newest, edk2-stable202608, predates it, and the advisory still lists the patched version as "Not patched currently." Microsoft's Project Mu has already pulled the fix into its release branches, and cut tagged builds on October 26.

Even with the fix public in source, a server operator has nothing to install until the maker of their firmware ships a BIOS or UEFI update built from it. That step is at least straightforward, Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at the firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars Technica: unlike Secure Boot bypasses such as BootHole and BlackLotus, the flaw "can be fixed with a basic code fix" and does not require certificate or key revocations.

Until that update arrives, the advisory lists no workaround. Because the flaw can only be reached during a network boot, operators who do not need PXE can disable it to reduce exposure. Ars also advised watching boot-time network traffic and logs for signs of attempts.

How It Became Public

The flaw was found by Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes-Mitra of Google, the advisory credits. A coordinated disclosure had been planned for January 2027.

That plan was overtaken on September 28, when a pull request to EDK II, signed off by an AMI engineer, publicly described the flaw by its CVE number and included the fix. Once the people who found it saw the post, TianoCore published its advisory on October 22, weeks before the planned date.

With the patch public, Ars noted that skilled attackers can study it to determine how the flaw is triggered and build working exploits.

There is no sign the flaw has been used in an attack. It was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of its October 27 update, and no researcher has reported seeing it exploited.

The flaw is also not, on its own, a way into a network, Ars Technica reported after putting questions to several firmware researchers. The realistic attacker is an insider, or someone who has already gained a low-level foothold on the local network and wants to dig deeper.

"An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint's TPM," said HD Moore, the creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at the security firm Dragos, in comments to Ars Technica.

"This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario)."

It is not the first serious flaw in EDK II's network-boot code. In January 2024, researchers disclosed PixieFail, a set of nine flaws in the same part of EDK II, also reachable during PXE boot. Ars reported that fuzzing projects started after PixieFail to find more bugs in the code did not catch this one.

item.title: Hackers Target Critical Oracle E-Business Suite RCE Flaw Days After Security Patch (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors are beginning to probe for a newly patched critical vulnerability in Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS), according to threat intelligence firm Defused Cyber.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS score: 9.8) , a case of improper authentication in the Oracle Application Object Library of Oracle E-Business Suite. It was patched by Oracle last week as part of its Critical Patch Update.

Security researchers Brandon Peterson, Jimi Sebree, and Noah King of Horizon3.ai have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw to Oracle on July 24, 2026.

"Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, October 27," Defused Cyber said in an X post.

In an advisory for the vulnerability, Horizon3.ai described it as an unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability that could be chained to achieve remote code execution.

"The vulnerability allows an attacker with network access to the affected Thin Client Framework (TCF) servlet to execute SQL as the APPS database user, then run operating system commands as the EBS application account," the cybersecurity company said.

Specifically, an attacker can issue a crafted request to the vulnerable TCF servlet at "/OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer" to run SQL with the privileges of the APPS database user and ultimately enable system command execution with the privileges of the EBS application account.

Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-101767 can permit an attacker to read or modify application data accessible to APPS and execute commands on the application host.

"Depending on the deployment, affected data may include financial, payroll, HR, and procurement records. Operating system access is governed by the permissions of the compromised EBS application account," Horizon3.ai warned.

While internet-facing EBS deployments present the most risk, internal EBS systems can also be exploited if an attacker can reach the vulnerable servlet from a compromised system or another accessible network segment.

Users are advised to update to the latest version as soon as possible. If immediate patching is not an option, the following workarounds can be applied -

  • Remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, associated with oracle.apps.fnd.tcf.SocketServer, from the EBS URL firewall allowlist.
  • Restrict access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks.
  • Monitor the EBS application host and database for signs of compromise.

Horizon3.ai has also shared the below indicators of compromise -

  • Unauthenticated POST requests to /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer that instantiate the Gantt data-server class (oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer), followed by backend database activity.
  • SQL reconnaissance shortly after unauthenticated web requests (database version, current user, directory objects).
  • Unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account spawning /bin/sh via the Concurrent Manager to run OS commands.

Vulnerabilities in EBS are a hot target for attackers. Over the past year, two critical flaws in the same product (CVE-2025-61882 and CVE-2026-46817, CVSS scores: 9.8) have come under active exploitation, with the former leveraged by the Cl0p ransomware and extortion crew.

item.title: PHP2Shell Attack Roots 25 Servers, Breaches U.S. Government-Affiliated Network (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what appears to be an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted attack orchestrated by a suspected China-nexus threat actor that has leveraged the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to breach exposed systems.

The activity, which was observed on October 25, 2026, involved an attacker combining PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including three systems in a U.S. government-affiliated environment.

"The affected devices run specific versions of a large vendor's firewall software," cybersecurity firm Dream said. "The attacker then launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration."

The name of the affected vendor was not disclosed, but the Israeli company said it notified the entity. The attack chain essentially brings together two sets of vulnerabilities impacting PHP and the Linux kernel -

  • PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2) that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution
  • Fragnesia, a Linux kernel local privilege escalation vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-46300 (CVSS score: 7.8)

"The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell," Dream researchers explained. "It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform."

"The vulnerability targets PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the firewall's appweb management server. The firewall OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack."

The custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain, coupled with CVE-2026-46300, is said to have rooted 25 servers across the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

Artifacts discovered by Dream indicate that the operation started with exploit development in a lab environment before obtaining persistent access to a U.S. government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

"Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a U.S. government-affiliated environment," the company noted.

The links to AI-assisted tooling stem from evidence pointing to the installation of Anthropic's Claude Code in the attack infrastructure, along with the presence of API keys for FOFA and an AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan configured with large language models (LLMs) from DeepSeek and Kimi.

What's more, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across nearly 40 scripts suggest the use of AI to augment the development process. The entire operation, per Dream, unfolds as follows -

  • Attacker uses FOFA to identify approximately 19,000 internet-facing firewalls with exposed management interfaces worldwide.
  • A custom version scanner is executed to determine which among those devices are online and what operating system version they are running. About 5,000 devices respond with the version information.
  • The attacker filters the servers to those located in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and then limits the scope to systems that match newer release branches running PHP 8.0.30. This step yields 240 targets.
  • The target list is fed as input to an automated batch runner that exploits the PHP2Shell-Fragnesia chain, plants a PHP web shell on a publicly accessible directory on the firewall, verifies root access, and logs the target's hostname and IP to a CSV file. This step allows the attacker to gain root access to 24 servers.
  • Two of the successfully compromised systems are identified as belonging to a U.S. government-affiliated organization. One of them crashes shortly after it was rooted on October 23, 2026, at 6:14 p.m. UTC and never comes back online. The attacker carries out a dedicated campaign to successfully root a second system on October 24, 2026, at 10:09 a.m. UTC.
  • The attacker exploits the second system to build a persistent channel into the internal network via a reverse SSH tunnel connecting the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure. At 11:35 a.m. UTC, a third government server is compromised using the same method, the only difference being that this was an internal firewall management server only reachable through the tunnel. The total number of rooted servers reaches 25.
  • The attacker targets Active Directory to decrypt the LDAP service account password, enumerate users, and spray passwords against every user account using organization-themed passwords in an attempt to extract credentials. The operation also attempts to create backdoor Active Directory accounts.

It's unclear if the activity allowed the threat actor to successfully find valid credentials or create backdoor accounts. As a result, the full extent of the compromise remains indeterminate.

"Since [the] U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts," Dream said.

"The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization's identity infrastructure. The 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked with active web shells. The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running. And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional OS versions."

The disclosure comes as the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities have witnessed only limited exploitation in the wild, with threat actors highlighting the challenges in converting a proof-of-concept (PoC) into a reliable attack vector against real targets despite integrating them into their campaigns.

"In practice it's unexploitable crap. To exploit real targets you need the offsets from libphp.so, which are unique to every build and impossible to brute-force. You can reproduce it on your own test bench, or if you already have access to the target's file system," a member who goes by the handle c0d3x on the XSS forum said, according to Flare.

item.title: Researcher Reveals How Logic Bugs Alone Cracked Microsoft Edge in $175,000 Pwn2Own Win (2026)
item.description:
A chain of logic flaws, with no memory corruption, can turn a malicious web page into code running on a Windows computer outside Microsoft Edge's sandbox, a security researcher has shown.

Orange Tsai of DEVCORE published the full method on October 28, five months after the chain won $175,000 at the Pwn2Own Berlin contest in May. Microsoft fixed the Edge bugs the day after the contest, so an up-to-date browser is not at risk.

A browser sandbox is the wall that keeps a web page's code inside the browser and off the rest of the computer. Breaking out of it, and then running a program, is what turns a web bug into full control of the machine.

Browser escapes like this almost always rely on memory corruption. This one used none. In his write-up, Tsai describes a chain built solely from logic errors in how Edge and Windows handle ordinary features, and he says the whole exploit is under 100 lines of code.

The result is a universal cross-site scripting (UXSS) primitive: a way to run JavaScript on any website, bypassing the content security policy meant to prevent it.

Because the attack starts from the browser's own process, it can reach sites like google.com that an ordinary web bug cannot touch. Tsai calls this a new attack surface rather than a one-off bug.

This was a competition exploit, not an attack seen in the wild. Tsai demonstrated it on stage at Pwn2Own; there is no evidence it has been used against real users, and the public CVE records list exploitation as none. One step in the chain restarts the browser, which Tsai notes is a convenience for the contest and not needed in a real attack.

The chain begins with an Edge feature for business sign-ins called a conditional access navigation throttle. Tsai found that triggering it lets the browser's own process start a new navigation that is not tied to the page that asked for it, so Edge attaches it to whichever tab is open. That mismatch is the first bug, and it produces the UXSS.

Making it run without a click took four more weaknesses. Edge checked that the request came from a trusted Microsoft site, but Tsai bypassed the check by opening the request from a second window. Edge's popup blocker should have stopped that window, but Edge carried a hardcoded list of allowed addresses, and one of them opened the popup.

The attack also required the victim to be already signed in, which the Edge auto-sign-in feature provides on its own when the user visits a Microsoft site. Lastly, the chain reads the victim's email address from a Microsoft site, assets.msn.com, which returned it to any website due to a misconfigured cross-origin setting.

Running JavaScript everywhere is still not in control of the computer. To escape the sandbox, Tsai used Edge's reading mode, Immersive Reader, which runs under a custom read:// address that Microsoft left off the list of pages barred from running scripts.

From there, the chain called an internal Edge function meant to zip up diagnostic logs and abused it to write a file with an attacker-chosen name and content anywhere on disk.

That file write is turned into code execution in two steps. The chain overwrites a configuration file that controls which websites may launch which protocol handlers, then restarts Edge so the file is read. It then launches a telnet:// link; because Windows does not ship a telnet program by default, it searches the system path for one and runs an attacker-planted copy from a folder the low-privileged user can write to.

Microsoft shipped the fix on May 15, the day after the contest, in Edge Stable version 148.0.3967.70. That release carried three Edge-specific fixes, tracked as CVE-2026-45492, CVE-2026-45494, and CVE-2026-45495. The first is recorded as a security feature bypass, and the second as a spoofing bug, both affecting Edge versions before 148.0.3967.70.

Microsoft's records rate the first two at 5.4 on a 10-point scale, a medium score that reflects a single bug in isolation, not the full chain that strings them into code execution. DEVCORE said the fix came within 24 hours of the disclosure.

Updating Edge closes this chain. Because the fix shipped in May, a browser on automatic updates has long since received it, and no separate action is needed.

Tsai built the chain by hand, over about two months, without any AI help, and frames the work as a point about where human research still matters. "The hard part is finding them, and once you find them all, chaining is the easiest part," he writes of the logic bugs. The research won the 2026 Pwnie Award for Epic Achievement.

item.title: Google to Allow One-Tap Android App Installs From Approved Third-Party Stores Outside U.S. (2026)
item.description:
Third-party Android app stores can now apply to Google for permission to install apps with one tap, without Android's usual confirmation screens, and to update them in the background.

To qualify, a store must pass identity checks and send Google its full catalog, along with every new app and update, for ongoing malware scanning. Approved stores get the features from December 1, but only on devices running Android 17 QPR2 or later in supported countries, which do not include the US.

Today, a user installing apps from a third-party store must first enable the store to install apps, then confirm each install and each update. From December 1, a store in Google's Registered App Stores program gets that permission automatically once it is approved, and its updates run in the background under the user's own update settings.

Google announced the program in March, alongside changes it said resolved its disputes with Epic Games. Joining is optional, and stores that stay out will continue to operate as they do today.

Under Google's rules, the store must still get the user's explicit consent for each install and "must not install apps silently without user consent." Large downloads and background installs must show a visible notification while they run.

If an install is started on another device, the store must show a notification that does not close automatically.

IT administrators can block registered stores from being installed on managed devices. Google's program pages do not say whether the block also applies to a store that is already installed.

Beyond the catalog scanning, Google's requirements say a store must:

  • be registered as an organization and keep its developer identity verified under Android developer verification, Google's identity check for app developers
  • send every version of its own app to Google for malware screening, exactly matching the version it publishes on the web and through other channels
  • work to keep malware and other potentially harmful apps out of its catalog
  • fix major security flaws that come to its attention
  • not block other app stores from being installed, interfere with them, or hide or change Android's security notifications
  • pay a $10,000 yearly fee, due before Google starts its review

Each store stays responsible and liable for everything in its catalog. Google won't moderate the content in registered stores.

If more than 1% of install attempts or more than 2% of a store's apps are found to be potentially harmful over a 30-day period, Google charges additional fees to screen and clean up the catalog.

A store that fails to meet any requirement, including paying on time, can be removed from the program until the issue is resolved. Google gives notice and a chance to fix it first.

Google's program pages do not describe how submitted apps are scanned, how quickly new uploads are checked, or what results the checks produce.

Registered stores also get a Google tool, the Android Developer ID API, to check whether each app in their catalog comes from a verified developer and can be installed. Google recommends that stores block installs of apps that fail the check.

Android developer verification is a separate Google program, now in its first phase with seven app stores. Since September 30, certified Android devices in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand have checked that apps from those stores come from verified developers, according to Google. Google plans to extend the checks worldwide in 2027.

Availability follows each user's home country. Short trips to unsupported countries do not turn off one-tap installs or automatic updates.

Android 17 QPR2 is one of Android's quarterly platform releases (QPRs). Its latest version, released October 16, is still a beta, and Google's release notes give no date for the final release.

In the US, a separate Google program for distributing third-party stores through Google Play has been in effect since July 22.

item.title: Volt Typhoon Used Covert Silent Train Network in Four Zero-Day Exploitation Campaigns (2026)
item.description:
The China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Volt Typhoon has been attributed to a now-disrupted covert access network dubbed Silent Train that has been put to use for zero-day exploitation and strategic access.

"First identified in late 2023, Silent Train uses rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise infrastructure," Lumen Technologies Black Lotus Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "It employs anti-forensic techniques, compartmentalized operations, and post-operation cleanup to minimize detection and attribution."

Its main purpose is to facilitate critical attack phases like vulnerability exploitation, credential access, data exfiltration, and to maintain continued access to victim environments. The activity stands out for two main reasons -

  • It singled out entities that could provide scalable access to downstream customers, sensitive networks, or strategic programs.
  • It targeted endpoint management platforms, network management systems, SD-WAN orchestrators, and control plane technologies that play a crucial role within enterprise environments.

Hundreds of victims have been identified across telecommunications providers, government, defense contractors, satellite and mission-critical communication services, universities, IT firms, and critical infrastructure such as water, energy, transportation, maritime, rail, aviation, and emergency services.

Volt Typhoon (aka Bronze Silhouette, Insidious Taurus, UNC3236, Vanguard Panda, and Voltzite) is the moniker assigned to a China-linked state-sponsored group known for its targeting of critical infrastructure networks, particularly communications, energy, transportation, and water and wastewater systems sectors.

Known to be active since at least 2021, the threat actor was previously observed exploiting a file upload vulnerability in Versa Director as a zero-day (CVE-2024-39717) to deliver a bespoke web shell called VersaMem designed to harvest credentials and enable access to downstream customers.

Silent Train session chains through multiple non-U.S. and U.S. hops

The latest findings from Black Lotus Labs show that the security flaw was one among four confirmed zero-day campaigns the threat actor has conducted through Silent Train. The remaining three vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 - A set of insecure deserialization and command injection vulnerabilities in N-able N-central
  • CVE-2026-20127 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Controller
  • CVE-2026-16812 - An operating system command injection vulnerability in Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator

Separately, Volt Typhoon is also suspected to have taken advantage of a likely zero-day vulnerability in Quest KACE before it was patched in October 2025. The campaign is estimated to have impacted more than 30 victims.

"Silent Train is built around rapidly rotating chains of compromised SOHO, IoT, and enterprise devices that are exploited on demand, used against carefully selected targets, cleaned up after each operation, and continuously refreshed," Black Lotus Labs said.

"This model has enabled Volt Typhoon to conduct exploitation and post-exploitation operations with exceptional operational security while minimizing opportunities for detection, attribution, and disruption."

A defining characteristic of these attacks is the repeated targeting of systems that can open the door to broad visibility, control, and access across large enterprise environments of strategic value to the U.S.

What's interesting is that the covert access capability began to take shape sometime around November 2023, just weeks before the first round of disruption targeting KV-botnet, an IoT botnet linked to multiple China-nexus state-sponsored threat actors, including Volt Typhoon.

Silent Train's operational activity is said to have surged in the wake of the botnet's second disruption in late January 2024, while simultaneously shifting to an ephemeral infrastructure comprising diverse device types and across geographies.

"Rather than continue using persistent infrastructure, Volt Typhoon shifted to a model using one-time-use chains of compromised devices that it could rebuild as needed," Black Lotus Labs said. "Volt Typhoon rapidly assembled and dismantled transient infrastructure, creating a resilient, secure, and compartmentalized framework that protected valuable access."

Sector distribution of organizations targeted through Silent Train

Described as a "layered, multi-hop framework," Silent Train is designed to let Volt Typhoon operators relay malicious traffic through several devices before it reaches the targets so as to obscure its origins from both victims and defenders. Each link in the chain serves a specific purpose -

  • Virtual private servers (VPS) that function as a temporary staging area and allow threat actors to provision and discard them after each session. The sessions begin from VPS infrastructure located outside the U.S.
  • Compromised non-U.S. SOHO and IoT devices located across different countries, providers, and hardware that conceal the starting point of the attack.
  • U.S.-based compromised devices that function as an exit node before reaching the domestic victim and help evade geofencing and IP reputation blocklists.

No less than 27 device classes, ranging from SOHO and IoT devices (e.g., TP-Link, Intelbras, Ruckus Wireless, SATO, NETGEAR, Zyxel, and Cambium) to enterprise platforms (e.g., Fortinet, Cisco, PRTG, Mirth Connect, and CyberPanel), have been exploited and enrolled into the covert network.

"Silent Train stands out for its operational discipline, focusing on short-lived, selfmanaged sessions rather than persistent relays or C2 infrastructure," Black Lotus Labs said. "To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node."

"This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and 'live off the land' utilities. At the end of operational sessions, they removed every artifact and dismantled the operational chain in their wake. Silent Train sessions lasted about four hours on average, with some lasting only minutes."

Another notable aspect is the designation of certain device types to specific positions within Silent Train. For instance, Intelbras modems have been found to only appear as relay nodes, while Netgear Orbi and Fortinet FortiGate appliances served as U.S.-based intermediary and exit points responsible for interacting with the victim.

Put differently, the infrastructure points to deliberate compartmentalization across layers, confining some device types to certain roles that remain constant while the underlying infrastructure itself changes over time so as to complicate attribution efforts.

By early 2025, however, Silent Train is believed to have evolved from a completely ephemeral relay network to a hybrid architecture that retained enterprise-grade devices for an average of one to three months instead of changing them after each engagement.

Subsequent maturation of the platform introduced reverse-tunnel variants that used open-source proxies like Chisel and FRP to send traffic from infected devices to upstream infrastructure.

Within the U.S., Hawaii, California, and Texas have emerged as the focus areas of Silent Train operations, which boils down to the fact that these states host major military installations, telecommunications infrastructure, defense contractors, satellite communications providers, and critical logistics networks.

"Victimology indicates deliberate efforts to maintain access to critical ecosystems that support defense, logistics, communications, military and civilian operations, especially during heightened tensions or crises in the Indo-Pacific region," Black Lotus Labs said.

"The resulting picture is one of a highly structured framework built to acquire, protect, and sustain strategic access at scale. Through repeated targeting of centralized management platforms and control plane technologies, Silent Train shows how Volt Typhoon systematically pursues and preserves access to some of the most consequential networks in the United States."

item.title: Attackers Exploit PHP2Shell Flaws in Internet-Exposed Palo Alto Networks Management Interfaces (2026)
item.description:
Palo Alto Networks on Wednesday warned that threat actors are exploiting the recently patched PHP2Shell vulnerabilities against publicly-accessible management interfaces.

"Active exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface exposed to the internet," the network security company said in an update to its advisory.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2), allow attackers to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on systems running affected versions of PHP. The issues were patched upstream by the PHP Foundation on October 21, 2026, in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

The development comes days after Israeli cybersecurity company Dream said it observed a suspected China-nexus threat actor weaponizing the flaws in conjunction with a local privilege escalation bug in the Linux kernel, tracked as Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300, CVSS score: 7.8), to root 25 servers across the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

Among those were three systems belonging to a U.S. government-affiliated environment.

"The affected devices run specific versions of a large vendor's firewall software," Dream noted. "The attacker then launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration."

Although Dream did not disclose the name of the affected firewall vendor, the timing of the advisory, combined with the fact that other network security companies have not reported malicious exploitation against their products, suggests that these events may be related.

The Hacker News has contacted both Dream and Palo Alto Networks for comment, and we will update the story if we hear back.

The development has prompted the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to add CVE-2026-46300 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 31, 2026.

"This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 to implant PHP web shells and run commands as root," CISA said.

Palo Alto Networks has also noted that no special configuration is required to be affected by this issue, adding the risk is highest on PAN-OS when access to the management interface is allowed from external IP addresses on the internet.

"This issue strictly affects the management web interface, which includes the HTTPS web UI and XML API service," it said. "It affects the dataplane interface only if a management profile is attached to it."

The following versions of PAN-OS are impacted by PHP2Shell -

  • PAN-OS 12.2
    • < 12.2.4-h1 (Fixed in >= 12.2.4-h1)
  • PAN-OS 12.1
    • < 12.1.4-h13 (Fixed in >= 12.1.4-h13) (ETA: 10/29)
    • < 12.1.7-h11 (Fixed in >= 12.1.7-h11)
    • < 12.1.10-h3 (Fixed in >= 12.1.10-h3) (ETA: 10/30)
  • PAN-OS 11.2
    • < 11.2.4-h23 (Fixed in >= 11.2.4-h23) (ETA: 10/30)
    • < 11.2.7-h23 (Fixed in >= 11.2.7-h23)
    • < 11.2.10-h16 (Fixed in >= 11.2.10-h16)
    • < 11.2.13-h4 (Fixed in >= 11.2.13-h4)
    • < 11.2.16-h1 (Fixed in >= 11.2.16-h1)
  • PAN-OS 11.1
    • < 11.1.4-h38 (Fixed in >= 11.1.4-h38)
    • < 11.1.6-h40 (Fixed in >= 11.1.6-h40)
    • < 11.1.7-h12 (Fixed in >= 11.1.7-h12) (ETA: 10/30)
    • < 11.1.10-h36 (Fixed in >= 11.1.10-h36)
    • < 11.1.13-h16 (Fixed in >= 11.1.13-h16)
    • < 11.1.16-h4 (Fixed in >= 11.1.16-h4)
  • PAN-OS 10.2
    • < 10.2.7-h39 (Fixed in >= 10.2.7-h39) (ETA: 10/30)
    • < 10.2.10-h42 (Fixed in >= 10.2.10-h42) (ETA: 10/29)
    • < 10.2.13-h27 (Fixed in >= 10.2.13-h27)
    • < 10.2.16-h12 (Fixed in >= 10.2.16-h12)
    • < 10.2.18-h13 (Fixed in >= 10.2.18-h13)

  • Route incoming traffic for the MGT port through a DP port, e.g., enabling management profile on a DP interface for management access.
  • Replace the Certificate for Inbound Traffic Management.
  • Decrypt inbound traffic to the management interface so the firewall can inspect it.
  • Enable threat prevention on the inbound traffic to management services.

"The security risk posed by this issue on PAN-OS and Panorama is minimized by restricting access to the management interface to only trusted internal IP addresses according to our recommended best practice deployment guidelines."

item.title: China-Linked Hackers Exploited VMware ESX Zero-Day to Reduce Audit Trail Visibility (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added a security flaw impacting Broadcom VMware ESX to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, after CrowdStrike revealed that it had been weaponized by a China-nexus threat actor known as Warp Panda in attacks targeting the U.S. legal sector.

The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-41709 (CVSS score: 2.7), an a case of insufficient logging that could permit permit a malicious actor with admin access to perform certain operations without being logged.

In an advisory released in July 2026, Broadcom revealed that the issue was addressed in the following versions -

  • VMware Cloud Foundation SXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 and ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025
  • VMware vSphere Foundation SXi-9.1.0.0-25370933 and ESXi-9.0.2.0100-25595025
  • VMware ESX ESXi80U3j-25429389
  • VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.4
  • VMware Telco Cloud Platform ESXi80U3j-25429389

The development comes in response to CrowdStrike's 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report, which revealed that Warp Panda had exploited CVE-2026-41709 as a zero-day in early 2026 with an aim to reduce audit trail visibility.

Warp Panda "exploits internet-facing edge devices using zero-day vulnerabilities and custom malware to maintain covert, persistent access," it said in the report shared with The Hacker News, adding the adversary "actively circumvents detection by bypassing audit logging, harvesting cloud session tokens, and registering rogue multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices."

The threat actor, also tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), Clay Typhoon, and VerdantBamboo, has a storied history of weaponizing zero-day vulnerabilities in Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure devices.

Earlier this month, Google-owned Mandiant also attributed the hacking crew to the zero-day exploitation of a critical improper origin validation flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deliver malware families like SAWFLY and BARECLAW.

Attacks mounted by Warp Panda involve the exploitation of internet-facing edge devices to obtain initial access, after which the threat actor pivots to VMware vCenter environments to deploy custom malware like BRICKSTORM and SharpStorm to maintain persistent access without attracting attention.

Select intrusions have also involved the targeting of cloud services with an aim to extract user session tokens to access Microsoft 365 environments sans raising any credential-based alerts. In at least one case, Warp Panda is said to have registered a new MFA device on a compromised account as a way to set up persistent access even if the password is changed. 

"Warp Panda represents a sustained and strategically focused China-nexus cyber espionage threat to U.S. entities across multiple sectors, including the legal sector," CrowdStrike said.

"The legal sector's concentration of client communications, merger and acquisition materials, active litigation strategy, and cross-client access makes it a high-value collection target for a state-directed adversary seeking intelligence with downstream operational utility."

In light of active exploitation of CVE-2026-41709, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are recommended to apply the fixes by November 11, 2026.

item.title: Hackers Exploited Cisco SD-WAN Flaw to Plant Malware Built to Steal Encryption Keys (2026)
item.description:
Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN flaw, fixed in February, to plant custom malware inside the systems that control an organization's SD-WAN network.

The malware, called KeyDrift, is designed to copy the keys that encrypt traffic between sites and store them for later use, Cisco Talos said on October 28. Talos calls the attacks historical but does not specify when they occurred or whether any keys were sent.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-20127 and has a CVSS score of 10.0. It allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to bypass authentication and gain administrative privileges on these control systems. On a Controller, the attacker can log in as a high-privileged internal account that is not root.

When Cisco disclosed the flaw in February, Talos tracked its exploitation as UAT-8616, a cluster of activity it said went back to at least 2023.

In Cisco's traditional key exchange, each SD-WAN router periodically generates an AES key for its traffic and sends it to the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart). The Controller passes the keys on to other routers. A process on the Controller called vdaemon runs the encrypted control connections that carry these keys.

On a compromised Controller, a KeyDrift component called LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted. For a preset list of edge routers, it pulls out their IP addresses and a 32-byte field. Talos assesses that field as the AES-256 key material that the Controller passes between routers.

LittleFilch encrypts what it collects with RSA and writes it to a file. It can then send that data over UDP to an address listed in a settings file, which it deletes after reading. Talos could not recover that settings file.

The group behind KeyDrift, which Talos tracks as UAT-11473, has targeted space and satellite services, defense and aerospace technology, and policy research.

The group's infrastructure "overlaps considerably" with Silent Train, Talos assesses with high confidence. Silent Train is the name Lumen's Black Lotus Labs uses for a network of hacked small-office, home-office, IoT and business devices.

Lumen says Volt Typhoon used the network to hide its activity. CISA, the NSA and the FBI said in 2024 that Volt Typhoon is a Chinese state-sponsored cyber group.

Talos links UAT-11473 to Volt Typhoon only through the infrastructure overlap. It does not say the two are the same group, or how UAT-11473 relates to UAT-8616, the cluster it reported in February.

Separately, Lumen said on October 28 that Volt Typhoon was exploiting CVE-2026-20127 by late 2025 and continued to exploit it after Cisco disclosed the flaw in February. Lumen does not tie that activity to KeyDrift.

KeyDrift primarily starts via modified runit scripts that Cisco SD-WAN devices use to launch their services, according to Talos. In one version, the script for the SSH service starts a loader script, conf_sshd, before the real SSH server. The conf_sshd script writes vdaemon's process IDs to a file, and a tool called rsshd injects KeyDrift's main module, PolyFlame, into each of those processes.

PolyFlame runs in memory inside vdaemon. It can act as a TinyShell-like backdoor that runs commands and reads and writes files, or as a relay that forwards commands between its command server and other machines. It is built to accept commands within SD-WAN control traffic, and the analyzed samples contained no hardcoded server address.

On a compromised Validator, formerly vBond, a fake aaamgr service under /etc/sv/aaamgr/ runs a packed loader, aaamgrd, that decrypts and runs PolyFlame. Cisco's real aaamgr component is a Python package and does not normally run as a compiled service.

There are also signs of timestomping: commands the group ran copied the timestamps and permissions of existing files onto its own files.

Affected Releases and Fixes

CVE-2026-20127 affects the Catalyst SD-WAN Controller (formerly vSmart), Manager (formerly vManage), and Validator (formerly vBond), regardless of their configuration. On-premises systems are affected, as are Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments, including the Cisco Managed and FedRAMP environments. Cisco added the Validator to its advisory on June 16.

Cisco says it is aware of limited exploitation of the flaw. There is no workaround, and the first fixed releases are:

Release train First fixed release
Earlier than 20.9 Migrate to a fixed release
20.9 20.9.8.2
20.11 20.12.6.1
20.12 20.12.5.3 or 20.12.6.1
20.13 20.15.4.2
20.14 20.15.4.2
20.15 20.15.4.2
20.16 20.18.2.1
20.18 20.18.2.1

Releases earlier than 20.9 and the 20.11, 20.13, 20.14 and 20.16 trains have reached end of software maintenance.

Until they can upgrade, on-premises customers can limit access to ports 22 and 830 to the IP addresses of known controllers and other known systems. Cisco says this step worked in a test environment, but that customers should check how well it works in their own networks. Such guardrails are already in place for Cisco's hosted SD-WAN cloud deployments.

Blocking the ports does not remove malware already on a device.

Checking for KeyDrift

Talos advises organizations to install Cisco's fixes, follow Cisco's Catalyst SD-WAN hardening guide and watch for signs of post-compromise activity. Anyone who finds such signs should start incident response and can ask Cisco's Technical Assistance Center (TAC) for help.

That advice does not say whether upgrading removes KeyDrift from a device that was already compromised, or whether any keys should be replaced. Cisco's February remediation guide for this flaw warns that there could be "existing exploits which are still in place" from before an upgrade.

KeyDrift uses these files and locations, some given only by name:

  • File: the run script under etc/sv/sshd/, modified to start conf_sshd
  • Directory: /etc/sv/aaamgr/, a fake service on a compromised Validator
  • File: aaamgrd, the packed loader
  • File: conf_sshd, the loader script
  • File: rsshd, the injector
  • File: libdssl.so, PolyFlame
  • File: libcommon.so, LittleFilch
  • File: /tmp/system-vdaemon, the list of vdaemon process IDs
  • File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin, LittleFilch's encrypted records
  • File: /var/tmp/vdaemon.conf, LittleFilch's send settings, deleted after reading

Talos's report does not include a list of file hashes, IP addresses or domains for KeyDrift.

Talos released Snort rules on October 28 that look for inbound KeyDrift command-and-control connections: 67387 through 67416 for Snort 2, and 7:44 through 7:73 for Snort 3. Rules 65938 and 65958, already available, cover CVE-2026-20127 itself.

The October 28 rule update lists the Snort 2 rules as disabled by default, so users of the paid Snort Subscriber rule set must turn them on. The Snort 3 rules appear with no default state.

To check for exploitation of the flaw itself, Cisco says to look in /var/log/auth.log for Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin entries from unknown IP addresses. Before opening a TAC case, customers should run request admin-tech on each control component. The remediation guide also recommends rescanning those admin-tech files with the Check Bug Applicability feature on the Bug Search Tool page for bug CSCws52722.

For US federal civilian agencies, CISA's February 25 emergency directive sets out what to do if a root account compromise is found. They must report it to CISA, deploy fresh Manager, Controller and Validator instances from patched images, and move their edge routers to the new systems.

item.title: Attacker Tried to Exploit Alpine Linux’s GitLab via CVSS 10.0 Flaw Its Ruby Left Open (2026)
item.description:
An attacker tried to exploit a critical GitLab vulnerability on the Alpine Linux project's own GitLab server a week after GitLab released a fix, Alpine Linux said on 28 October.

The flaw, CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS score: 10.0), can let an attacker run code on a GitLab server through a crafted regular expression in a CI configuration. Alpine found no evidence that the attack worked but cannot rule it out, so it rebuilt the server from scratch and reset every account's password.

GitLab's fix is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab ships in its own packages and container images. Alpine's GitLab image used standard Ruby, so upgrading the server to GitLab 19.3.6 on 22 October did not fix the flaw.

For anyone running GitLab on their own Ruby, built from source or in their own container image, "upgrading GitLab is not enough," Alpine said. Those servers also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later, and users of Alpine's alpinelinux/gitlab image need to pull 19.3.6 again.

The server gitlab.alpinelinux.org hosts aports, the repository from which Alpine's packages are built. Packages built from 20 to 24 October, and the 21 October releases, came from aports changes verified against records outside GitLab, according to Alpine.

Those releases include the minirootfs files that the official Alpine Docker images are built from. Alpine is extending the checks to 27 October, when it closed the server. The keys that sign its packages and releases have never been on the GitLab server.

How the Attack Unfolded

On 13 October, Alpine upgraded the server to GitLab 19.3.4 instead of 19.3.5, which it calls a mistake. The server was still on that version, without the 12 October fix, when a newly registered account began probing it on 20 October.

The account sent crafted CI configurations to the server on 20 and 21 October. They crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times, and the main attack on 21 October also caused 502 errors and caused CI jobs to fail.

In 4 of those crashes, the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step, according to Alpine. The attacker also downloaded Alpine's GitLab container image, which Alpine said: "suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build."

Alpine blocked the account on 23 October. The attacker came back on 25 and 26 October and tried to get back in, but those attempts failed, Alpine said.

On 26 October, Alpine found that the server was still vulnerable after its 22 October upgrade to 19.3.6. The next day, it closed GitLab to everyone except its developers and build servers and started rebuilding it.

The rebuild finished on 28 October. Alpine also replaced GitLab's secret keys, and the rebuilt server runs Ruby 3.3.13 or later, which has the fix. Alpine is testing it before reopening it to the public.

What Alpine Can and Cannot Rule Out

Alpine found no sign that the attacker's code ran on the server. Timing probes showed no delays;; there were no unexpected files, keys, hooks, or processes; and no private data was sent back to the attacker via any web or API request that Alpine can see.

It cannot be sure, though. "A successful exploit would leave no crash and no trace in the web logs," Alpine said. Some logs from the attack day are gone, including background job logs and the old container's filesystem, and neither Alpine nor its hosting provider logged outbound network connections.

Because the evidence needed to confirm code execution no longer exists, Alpine treated the server as compromised and rebuilt it to remove any foothold a successful exploit could have left.

If the attack succeeded, these could have been exposed:

  • Email addresses, names, and IP addresses of all users
  • Password hashes
  • 2FA secrets, CI/CD variables and runner tokens
  • Webhook, integration and push mirror credentials
  • Personal access tokens, which are stored as hashes
  • Private repositories, and confidential issues and merge requests

Beyond the password reset and the new secret keys, Alpine has not said whether runner tokens, CI/CD variables, access tokens or integration credentials stored on the server have been replaced.

To check its packages, Alpine confirmed that every aports change added from 20 to 22 October arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. It checked this against records it says the attacker could not reach: a developer's copy of the repository and all 45 build servers. Every package built from 20 to 24 October came from aports changes as published on git.alpinelinux.org.

Why the GitLab Upgrade Did Not Fix It

GitLab compiles the regular expressions in CI configurations with Ruby, and the bug behind CVE-2026-97229 is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby.

GitLab's 12 October release fixed it by patching the Ruby inside GitLab's Linux package and container images. Ruby's own fixed versions came out on 22 and 23 October.

A GitLab upgrade does not change a server's own Ruby, so a GitLab install on standard Ruby keeps the flaw until Ruby itself is updated to a fixed version, as Alpine found.

GitLab's fixed Linux packages and its official container images carry the patched Ruby. A self-compiled install, or a container image that installs Ruby separately as Alpine's did, does not get it.

As of 29 October, neither of GitLab's patch release posts for 12 and 21 October tells administrators of self-compiled installs to update Ruby. GitLab's self-compiled installation guide still lists Ruby 3.2 as its minimum version, and Ruby 3.2 reached end of life in April and will get no fix.

Which GitLab Servers Are Exposed

GitLab's advisory says that, "under certain conditions," the flaw could have allowed an unauthenticated user to run code on the server. GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated are already patched.

Rapid7 built a working exploit in a lab and published proof-of-concept code on 13 October. The exploit ran commands as GitLab's git user on an unpatched official GitLab 19.4.1 image, but the same input did not run on the patched 19.4.2 image.

That exploit needs write access first: the attacker must commit a malicious .gitlab-ci.yml file and a file path with UTF-8 characters to a branch of a public project. That requirement does not apply on servers where new users can register themselves and create projects.

In Rapid7's tested route, "only the final CI lint request is unauthenticated." GitLab's own detection notes also say the attacker must first create that file path through ordinary repository APIs. Rapid7 does not yet know how the attack in the original report to GitLab, which is still private, avoids the write step.

Alpine has not said how its attacker's CI configurations reached GitLab, or whether new accounts could create public projects on its server.

CVE-2026-97229 was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the catalog's 28 October update.

What GitLab Administrators Should Do

GitLab's 21 October releases are the newest on each branch listed below, and they also fix CVE-2026-110264, a separate regex flaw.

Branch Fixes CVE-2026-97229, per GitLab's advisory Newest release (21 October)
19.5 Not listed as affected 19.5.1
19.4 19.4.2 19.4.3
19.3 19.3.5 19.3.6
19.2 19.2.8 19.2.9
19.1, 19.0 and 18.11 Not listed as affected 19.1.9, 19.0.10 and 18.11.13

Which release fixes a server depends on how GitLab is installed:

  • GitLab's Linux package or official container images: upgrade to the newest release for your branch.
  • Self-compiled installs, or images that install their own Ruby: upgrade GitLab and update Ruby to 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9, or later. Ruby 3.2 will not receive the fix, so servers running 3.2 need to upgrade to one of those versions.

GitLab's advisory named 19.3.4 as the fixed version for the 19.3 branch when it was published on 12 October. It now names 19.3.5 and lists 19.3.4 as affected, so servers still on 19.3.4 should move to 19.3.6.

If a server cannot be upgraded right away, Rapid7 suggests restricting anonymous access to public projects, stopping untrusted users from creating or writing to public projects, or blocking the CI lint route. Those steps cover only Rapid7's exploit route and do not fix the vulnerable regular expression compiler, the company said.

GitLab has published six detection rules for exploitation attempts against self-managed servers, written in the Sigma format. Four of them, which GitLab marks as experimental, look for hostile patterns in CI regexp warnings and GraphQL ciLint requests, unusually long file paths with non-ASCII characters, and Ruby crash reports that point to Onigmo.

The guidance with those rules warns that a successful exploit can leave no crash, and it gives these further steps:

  • Look for files owned by the git user in /tmp, unexpected child processes of Puma or Sidekiq, outbound connections, and changed crontabs or SSH keys for the git user.
  • If there are signs of code execution, treat the server as compromised and rotate the secrets in gitlab-secrets.json, all CI/CD variables, all runner tokens and all access tokens.
  • Limit who can create accounts and personal access tokens on the server.

What Alpine Users Should Do

Account holders will need to set a new password with "Forgot your password?" on the sign-in page when gitlab.alpinelinux.org reopens, Alpine said. It has also seen automated login attempts against its GitLab using passwords leaked from other sites, and anyone who used their gitlab.alpinelinux.org password elsewhere should change it there.

Users of the alpinelinux/gitlab image should pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on 27 October contains Ruby 3.3.13, while any 19.3.6 image pulled before then, and every older tag, is vulnerable.

Alpine's own Ruby packages already have the fix: Ruby 3.4.12 on Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge, and Ruby 3.3.13 on Alpine 3.21. Running apk upgrade installs it.

Ruby's maintainers say the bug matters only for programs that compile a regular expression from text an attacker controls, and that Ruby's Regexp.timeout setting does not protect against it.

item.title: GitHub Launches npm Firewall to Block Malicious Packages Before Installation (2026)
item.description:
GitHub has announced that it's introducing a new package firewall as a preview to block installation of suspicious npm packages during installation time.

"The firewall inspects both metadata requests and package downloads for signs of malicious activity, acting as an install-time policy gate," GitHub said.

The feature, which currently supports only npm packages, is available in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident GitHub Enterprise Cloud.

According to the Microsoft subsidiary, the firewall is placed between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories so as to deter malware attacks that compromise systems when packages are installed.

This behavior can expose users to severe security risks, especially when artificial intelligence (AI) agents and CI runners automatically install dependencies to complete a task or build without their explicit permission.

The idea is that endpoints like coding agents and CI/CD hosts use the firewall for their requests instead of directly pointing to the public package registries.  The firewall then checks package downloads against policy controls such as minimum package age and malware advisories, and blocks downloads that do not meet those policies.

To use the firewall, administrators are required to configure policy controls, such as the ones listed below -

  • Block known malware by checking against the GitHub Advisory Database for active malware advisories
  • Block packages based on the severity of vulnerabilities by checking the GitHub Advisory Database for flaws that affect the requested package version. The control defaults to "Critical only" as the severity level that blocks an installation, although users can choose "High or higher," "Medium or higher," or "Any severity."
  • Block attestation downgrades by comparing attestations for the requested package version with those of earlier versions and stop the download if the requested version does not have an SLSA attestation.
  • Block newly-introduced install scripts by checking whether the package recently added scripts that run using preinstall or postinstall hooks, which can be abused to steal sensitive data.

Block packages based on a cooldown period that prevents versions that are newer than the configured minimum age from being installed. The value can range from 1 to 365 days. The default value is 1 day. Users can disable it by setting it to 0.

Users who need access to a package that gets blocked erroneously by the firewall can submit an exception request, which can then be approved by enterprise administrators and security managers.

The development comes as Rust 1.100, which is scheduled for release on November 12, 2026, readies to add support for a configurable minimum publish age, allowing security scanners and maintainers time to flag and block malicious crate releases before they can be installed or used by users.

The value, defined via the "global-min-publish-age" option in "cargo/config.toml," allows users to specify a minimum publication age in days or weeks. If left unspecified, a seven-day waiting period is applied by default to skip releases published within that window.

Over the past year, similar waiting periods have been implemented across open-source ecosystems, including npm, Python, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Ruby, Bun, pnpm, and Yarn, as a way to bolster software supply chain security by reducing the chance that a newly published, unreviewed version is immediately pulled into a build.

Cooldown periods help add friction and slow down attacks in which a bad actor publishes a poisoned version of a popular package after seizing control of a maintainer account, thereby preventing rapid spread through manual or automated installations.

"The tradeoff is that legitimate fixes have to wait, too, unless developers make an exception," Socket said. "Malicious code also doesn't magically become harmless with age. A release that escapes detection can simply outlast the cooldown. The value is in buying researchers, maintainers, and registries time to act before the next dependency update carries an attack further."

item.title: Cisco Patches Actively Exploited ASA and FTD VPN Flaw That Can Crash Firewalls (2026)
item.description:
Cisco has released patches to address a high-severity security flaw in Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software that it said has been exploited in the wild.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76418, is rated 8.6 on the CVSS scoring system. Successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

According to Cisco, the issue is rooted in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of ASA and FTD software.

"This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group," it said in a Wednesday advisory. "An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition."

The network equipment major said it became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability in October 2026, but did not share any specifics as to when the attacks began, who is behind them, and the scale of the efforts.

Fixes for the flaw are available in the following versions -

item.title: 26,400 Valid Cloud and AI Credentials Found Exposed in Public Gitee Repositories (2026)
item.description:
26,400 credentials that developers left in public code on Gitee, a Chinese code-hosting service, still worked when a researcher tested them. Anyone who copied one from that code could have used it.

Independent researcher Ben Zimmermann found them by scanning 7.25 million public Gitee repositories and reported the results on October 28. Most were keys for cloud and AI services, led by 9,473 Alibaba Cloud AccessKey pairs.

Zimmermann sent the vendors with the most exposed keys a list of their credentials, but he did not contact the developers who leaked them. When he published, he had not confirmed that any of the reported credentials had been revoked. So anyone who has pushed a key to a public Gitee repository cannot assume it has been revoked.

The scan ran for about a month, but Zimmermann did not provide the dates, so it is unclear how long ago the credentials were tested. He also did not say whether anyone else had used them.

He ran two secret scanners, TruffleHog and Kingfisher, over every repository. Both tried each credential against the service that issued it and kept only those that worked, he wrote.

The scanners read each repository's full commit history. A key that a developer later removed from the code could still be found and counted there.

The 26,400 figure counts each credential once, regardless of how many repositories it appeared in. By commit date, 12,242 of the credentials came from 2025, nearly half the total. Some dated to the late 2000s.

What Was Exposed

After the Alibaba Cloud keys, the largest groups were 3,805 YouTube API keys, 3,170 DeepSeek keys, 1,489 keys for Zhipu's BigModel AI platform, and 1,348 OpenAI keys. Smaller numbers were found for GitHub, AWS, Google Cloud and Google's Gemini.

One of the credentials was "an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform," Zimmermann wrote. He did not name the platform or say what the credential could reach.

What a working key lets someone do depends on the service. OpenAI says that a compromised key allows another person to use the account's quota without the owner's consent. That can cause "data loss, unexpected charges," a used-up monthly quota, and interrupted API access.

A YouTube API key is a Google Cloud API key that identifies a project, Google says. Without API restrictions, such a key can be used with every API that accepts Google Cloud keys.

What to Do If You Committed Keys

Treat any key that has ever been in a public Gitee repository as exposed, and revoke it at the provider. Deleting a key from the code or rewriting the repository's history does not revoke it, as noted by TruffleHog's maker, Truffle Security.

  • Alibaba Cloud: create a new AccessKey pair, switch your apps to it, then disable and delete the old pair. Check for unexpected charges and for resources created or deleted that you did not need, Alibaba Cloud's leak response plan says. ActionTrail shows the key's API calls for the last 90 days, but data operations in services such as OSS and SLS have to be checked in each service's own logs.
  • Google and YouTube API keys: rotate the key, which creates a new key with the same restrictions, update your apps to use it, then delete the old key. Add API restrictions so the key works only with the APIs you need.
  • OpenAI: rotate the key immediately from the API Keys page, as OpenAI advises, and set spend limits to help limit charges from a leaked key.

Two Scanners, Different Results

MongoDB makes Kingfisher, and Zimmermann's post was developed with its Kingfisher team.

In this scan, TruffleHog found 12,737 credentials that worked, and Kingfisher found 14,664, but only 1,001 were found by both. Each tool alone found about half of the total.

TruffleHog found almost all of the Alibaba Cloud keys. Kingfisher found all 1,489 BigModel keys, because TruffleHog has no detector for Zhipu's keys, Zimmermann wrote.

Teams that rely on a single scanner should verify its detectors against the services they use.

Gitee and Other Code Hosts

China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology chose Gitee in 2020 as the base for a national open-source code-hosting platform.

Gitee's public API is limited, and a 2021 attempt to study leaked credentials on the site gave up because of it.

Gitee's rate, 3.64 working credentials per 1,000 repositories scanned, is higher than the rates from earlier scans of GitLab (3.11) and Bitbucket (2.39). Those scans used only TruffleHog, Zimmermann wrote.

Based on TruffleHog's results alone, Gitee's rate is 1.76, but that count excludes services TruffleHog does not cover, such as Zhipu. So neither figure shows which platform leaks more.
