item.title: The Rise of the Threat Operator: How AI Will Redefine Security Operations and Careers (2026)
item.description:
AI is beginning to take over much of the work that has traditionally defined the security analyst's job. Investigating alerts, collecting evidence, correlating activity across tools, and executing response actions are becoming tasks that AI systems can perform on their own. As these capabilities mature, security operations centers (SOCs) will see major changes in how work is organized, how decisions are made, and what is expected of the people responsible for defending organizations.

For security professionals, this is a chance to take on a much broader role. As AI assumes more of the operational workload, analysts can move beyond individual alerts and investigations to direct the defense across the entire security lifecycle. We call this emerging role the Threat Operator: an AI-native security professional who translates business risk into defensive priorities, directs AI-driven operations, and exercises judgment over the decisions and actions taken by those systems.

The impact reaches beyond day-to-day SOC work. It will change the skills organizations need, how security professionals develop expertise, and the career paths open to people entering the field.

From Individual Tasks to Overall Defense

The traditional SOC developed around specialized functions, each supported by its own tools and workflows. Threat intelligence teams study adversaries, detection engineers create rules, threat hunters search for activity that existing controls may have missed, analysts investigate alerts, and incident responders contain confirmed threats. These functions are closely related, yet the work often moves between teams through separate systems, tickets, and manual handoffs. AI is starting to tie these activities together. For example, intelligence about a new threat can lead to a hunting hypothesis, which can reveal a detection gap and produce a new detection. That detection may identify suspicious activity requiring investigation, followed by containment and further improvements to the organization's defenses. AI agents can coordinate and execute these workflows, carrying context and findings from one stage to the next.

That changes where security professionals add the most value. A Threat Operator works across the defensive lifecycle, setting priorities based on the organization's exposure, business operations, and threat landscape. They determine which risks deserve attention, what the defense should accomplish, how much autonomy AI should have, and when a decision requires human intervention. They are also responsible for judging whether the operation is actually improving security.

Consider a financial institution facing a newly identified threat targeting identity infrastructure. AI agents could assess the institution's exposure, hunt for relevant activity, identify gaps in existing detections, and recommend defensive actions. The Threat Operator would provide the institutional context needed to guide that work, including which systems support critical business processes, what constitutes unacceptable risk, and which actions require authorization.

The result is a gradual shift from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop, with security professionals supervising and governing AI-driven operations. The level of autonomy will depend on the maturity of the technology, the consequences of particular actions, and the organization's tolerance for risk, but a human remains accountable throughout.

Rethinking How Security Professionals Gain Experience

Junior security analysts will feel some of the biggest effects. For decades, the SOC has provided an entry point into cybersecurity, with analysts developing their skills through alert triage, evidence collection, investigations, documentation, and escalation. Although much of this work is repetitive, it has also served as an apprenticeship. Over time, analysts learn how systems behave, how attackers operate, and how experienced practitioners distinguish genuine threats from benign activity. As AI absorbs more of these responsibilities, organizations will need to rethink how that experience is acquired. The traditional progression from handling simple alerts to managing complex investigations may become less relevant as AI takes on more sophisticated work. Without a deliberate approach to training, security teams may struggle to develop the experienced professionals they will need in the future.

AI can also open up a different path for professional development. Junior Threat Operators can gain supervised exposure to a much wider range of security activities, examining how intelligence informs hunting, how detections are developed, how investigations reach conclusions, and how response decisions affect the business. They can review the evidence behind AI-generated findings, challenge assumptions, identify missing context, and learn from the decisions made by more experienced colleagues. This only works if organizations invest in technical fundamentals and structured mentorship. Analysts still need to understand networks, operating systems, attacker techniques, and the security technologies underlying AI-driven workflows. Experienced practitioners will need to teach younger colleagues how to evaluate conclusions, recognize uncertainty, and exercise judgment when the available evidence is incomplete.

The Skills Needed

For the current generation of security analysts, technical proficiency has often been measured through familiarity with security tools and the ability to extract useful information from them. Query languages, detection logic, endpoint telemetry, and investigation techniques have been central to the profession. Those skills still matter. AI adds new demands on top of them: orchestration, governance, and interpreting automated decisions.

Threat Operators will need to translate business security risks into clear defensive objectives that AI systems can execute. They must understand the organization's architecture, critical assets, operational dependencies, and relevant adversaries, and know how to communicate that context to AI agents. Their work will involve evaluating hypotheses, validating evidence, setting escalation criteria, and determining whether an automated action has achieved its intended outcome.

For example, an AI system investigating a compromised server may recommend immediate isolation. That call could be technically sound. But the server may support a critical business process where disruption carries significant consequences. A Threat Operator must understand those dependencies and determine how the response should proceed, balancing containment requirements with operational risk. This need for defined oversight and accountability is also reflected in the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.

The role will combine four areas of expertise:

  • Business security risk: Understanding organizational priorities, critical assets, and the consequences of security decisions.
  • Threat and adversary understanding: Interpreting intelligence and anticipating how attackers may target the environment.
  • Defensive operations: Understanding detection, hunting, investigation, and response across the security lifecycle.
  • AI orchestration and judgment: Directing AI workflows, evaluating their conclusions, and governing automated actions.

Building a Career Path Around Defensive Outcomes

The Threat Operator role should become a career path with increasing levels of responsibility. Early-career operators can focus on validating evidence, reviewing AI conclusions, adding environmental context, and understanding how decisions connect across the defensive lifecycle. As they gain experience, they can begin translating business risks into defensive objectives, directing agent workflows, identifying coverage gaps, and determining when operations should escalate or act.

Senior Threat Operators will take responsibility for defining autonomy boundaries, governing consequential actions, evaluating the reliability of AI-driven decisions, and measuring whether security operations are reducing organizational risk. Professionals may enter this career path from investigations, threat intelligence, detection engineering, incident response, security architecture, or risk management, bringing different areas of expertise to a role that spans the entire defensive operation.

Security leaders should start building the training, governance, and progression frameworks needed to support these responsibilities. That includes establishing which decisions require human approval, how operators validate AI-generated evidence, how autonomy expands as systems demonstrate reliability, and how individual performance is evaluated. Measures such as the quality of defensive decisions, the closure of detection gaps, and improvements in threat coverage will matter more alongside traditional operational metrics.

This will happen at different speeds in different organizations. Security professionals will have more say in how their organizations defend themselves. The old SOC trained people to operate tools. The AI-native SOC has to train them to operate the defense.

Learn more about how Conifers helps security teams direct and govern AI-driven defense across the full SOC lifecycle.

item.title: Telegram Android Flaw Lets Attackers Run Code When Users Answer Voice Calls (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in Telegram for Android allowed an attacker to run code on a victim's phone via a voice call once the victim answered, according to security startup NebuSec.

The attacker needed only an ordinary Telegram account. Telegram fixed the flaw in version 12.10.4 of the app, released in late September, and NebuSec disclosed it on October 29.

The flaw can be triggered in every version from 8.6.2 through 12.10.3, NebuSec's co-founder and chief executive said in an email to The Hacker News. Those versions came out between March 2022 and September 2026.

The company confirmed it in private phone calls on ARM64-based phones and has no evidence so far that it directly affects Telegram's iOS and desktop apps or group calls.

Anyone using Telegram for Android should make sure the app is on version 12.10.4 or later. The version number appears at the bottom of the app's Settings page. The flaw had no CVE identifier as of October 29.

The Hacker News has asked NebuSec and Telegram whether the flaw was used in real attacks, and asked NebuSec what an attacker's code could reach on a phone.

During a Telegram call, the two apps send each other short messages to set up the call and report its state. One type, called MediaState, reports whether the microphone is muted, whether the camera is on, and how the video is rotated.

The flaw was in the code that reads MediaState messages. That code did not handle missing fields correctly and accessed memory it should not, according to NebuSec.

Telegram's published source code for version 12.10.3 contains a flaw that matches that description, a review by The Hacker News found. When a MediaState message included a rotation value, the code checked that value. It then read a different field, the video state, even if the message had no such field.

item.title: Webinar: How to Build AI Threat Readiness Into Your Security Operations (2026)
item.description:
Security teams have spent years trying to detect threats faster. AI is changing the harder part: how much time defenders have left to act.

Advanced AI models can now help attackers discover vulnerabilities, generate exploit code, and move through weaknesses faster than traditional security processes were built to handle.

The challenge is no longer just finding another vulnerability or generating another alert. It is knowing which exposures matter, what an attacker can reach, and which issues need to be fixed first.

That is the focus of next week's webinar, How to Build AI Threat Readiness Across Your Security Operations, featuring an expert from Wiz. The session will show how security teams can improve visibility, prioritize real risk, and shorten the path from detection to remediation.

Most security teams already have plenty of data. They have vulnerability findings, cloud alerts, identity signals, application telemetry, and threat detections. The harder problem is connecting those signals quickly enough to answer the questions that drive action.

Is this vulnerability reachable? Does the exposed asset contain sensitive data? Can an attacker move from it to something more important? Who owns the affected system? What should be fixed first?

When those answers live across different tools and teams, investigations slow down. That delay matters more when attackers can automate parts of the discovery and exploitation process.

📅 Save Your Spot Today: Register for the Webinar Here.

The webinar focuses on two practical needs: broad visibility and faster action.

Security teams need enough context to understand risk across cloud infrastructure, code, identities, SaaS, AI services, and the software supply chain. They also need a way to identify exploitable paths, investigate suspicious activity, and deliver remediation to the right owner without having to rebuild the same context every time.

A Wiz expert will explain how organizations can use unified security context to separate urgent exposure from background noise, understand attack paths, and bring security agents into investigation and remediation workflows.

For SOC teams, that can mean less time spent manually assembling context. For vulnerability management, it means knowing which findings deserve immediate attention. For cloud and security engineering teams, it means connecting risk to the people and systems that can actually fix it.

The goal is not to automate every security decision. It is to remove delays caused by fragmented tools, repetitive investigation, and unclear ownership.

Attendees will leave with a framework for assessing whether their current security operations are ready for faster, AI-assisted attacks. The key questions are practical: Can you see enough of the environment to understand an attack path? Can you quickly determine whether a new issue affects something attackers can reach? Can you move a validated risk from detection to remediation fast enough?

AI is increasing the speed at which weaknesses can be found and used. Security teams need to respond with better context and less delay.

item.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon Leads Benchmarks for Finding, Exploiting, and Patching Vulnerabilities (2026)
item.description:
Google on Wednesday took the wraps off Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.

"It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching," Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, said.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index benchmark, Carbon leads with a score of 59, surpassing Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 (58), OpenAI GPT-6 Astra (57), GPT-6.1 Sol (55).

One of the core focus areas is cybersecurity, where the latest iteration reportedly delivers significant performance improvements across the board, including vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. Carbon is also twice as likely to generate secure code versus Argon.

Google also emphasized that Carbon attempts to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks by seeking human input in the face of ambiguity rather than "guessing or forcing a path forward," as well as resisting every evaluated attack attempt at indirect prompt injection.

The debut of Gemini 4 Carbon comes less than a week after the tech giant unveiled Gemini 4 Argon. The release plan is similar to that of its predecessor, with the rollout currently limited to a subset of cyber defenders before expanding access to other trusted partners as part of its Fairwind Program.

Google also said it's actively engaged in the U.S. government's voluntary process for pre-release model testing.

The development comes as OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra, which it described as a fast, efficient model that "excels at communication and computer-based tasks."

"GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra," OpenAI said.

"GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user's task."

Earlier this week, rival Anthropic also disclosed that an unreleased, internal research model uncovered critical vulnerabilities in some of the world's most widely used software. 

This included a one-click remote code execution in Google Chrome, a one-click exploit chain in Apple Safari that could be used to access a user's browsing history, cookies, and other sensitive data, an Android lock screen bypass, and a denial-of-service (DoS) flaw in the Windows HTTP.sys driver (CVE-2026-33096, CVSS score: 7.5). All the identified issues have been fixed by Google, Apple, and Microsoft.

"These attack chains demonstrate the model's ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software," Anthropic said.

"These skills have historically been the domain of few specialist teams with expertise in these targets. Now, it’s something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

item.title: Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps Abuse Signed Executables to Deploy Crypto Miners (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors are delivering malicious loaders and cryptocurrency miners under the guise of artificial intelligence (AI) desktop applications for Anthropic Claude and OpenAI ChatGPT as part of a campaign dubbed Yoba.

The activity involves creating fake GitHub projects that claim to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus, only to deliver a malware family called YobaLoader.

"The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections," Check Point Research said in an analysis.

To add to the project's credibility, the attackers set up GitHub.io pages to describe the capabilities of the software. Although the GitHub projects' popularity is not manipulated using techniques like ghost networks, signs point to the use of SEO poisoning tactics to ensure that links to them are surfaced on top of search results on Google.

Some of the identified GitHub pages links are below -

  • github[.]com/gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop
  • gpt-5-6.github[.]io
  • github[.]com/gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io
  • github[.]com/gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io
  • gpt-6-astra[.]github[.]io
  • github[.]com/opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github[.]io
  • opus-5-0[.]github[.]io

"Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively," Check Point said. "This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor's true operational time zone."

Hosted within these repositories are ZIP archives that, among other files, contain two specific components -

  • Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI Codex or Claude executable
  • winmm.dll, a malicious DLL that's sideloaded by the executable

The DLL is a dropper codenamed YobaDropper, which implements checksum value checks by hashing the basename of its host executable and if it matches a hard-coded value "0xE6C2F326." In other words, the check requires it to be launched under "Setup.exe," and fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandboxed environment.

Additional anti-analysis techniques and pre-checks include 200,000 iterations of "Sleep(5500)," which amounts to 12.73 days, and skipping machines whose keyboard layout corresponds to that of Russia, Belarus, Tajikistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

Another language ID excluded from the infection process is Tatar. Notably missing from the list is Ukraine, which used to be historically included in such checks.

YobaDropper, for its part, triggers a DLL sideloading chain of its own comprising "wmpdmc.exe" and "ampdui.dll," copying the former from its "system32" folder and placing it in a new directory named "WMProcess" created under "ProgramData."

The dropper then extracts and decrypts an embedded payload, and drops it into the same folder as "wmpdui.dll." It also establishes persistence by means of a scheduled task that launches the legitimate executable to load the malicious payload.

The second DLL is YobaLoader. It implements the same anti-sandbox technique as YobaDropper, requiring the malware to be run only by "wmpdmc.exe" by checking the hash against a hard-coded value ("0x552751E3"). The loader is responsible for three main tasks -

  • Downloads an image from a Telegram channel ("t[.]me/yoba_fanclub").
  • Uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words and an integer value in the range 0–999 using a domain generation algorithm (DGA). The end result is domain in the format "adjective-noun-verb-digit.dedyn[.]io."
  • Queries Google's DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain a Base64-encoded command from a DNS TXT record by passing the constructed domain as input.
  • Decrypts the response to obtain the link to fetch the next-stage payload ("files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat").

"By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity," Check Point said.

The downloaded payload is then injected into "svchost.exe," resulting in the execution of an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.

Evidence indicates that the first GitHub repository was created around July 2026, although the malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August. What's more, early versions of YobaLoader have been found to only exclude Russia from infection, while also incorporating extensive anti-debugging and anti-VM checks, which have since been removed in newer versions.

"The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance," Check Point said. "By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious."
